[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Those granted favor are the prophets, whom God favored with prophethood. | mentions 19:58
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The people under divine anger are the Jews, whom God turned into apes and pigs; the requested path is other than their religion.
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r7] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The straying people are the polytheists, identified here as the Christians.
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8] MUQATIL, d. 150 · أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea.
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r9] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | Muqātil instructs a reader who reaches the closing words to say Āmīn; angels say it too, and if people's response coincides, the group's prior sins are forgiven.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh analyzes ghayr in 1:7 as an adjective meaning other than, not as an exceptive construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Amr ibn Maʿdīkarib's verse is paraphrased as كل أخ غير الفرقدين, with the ghayr phrase qualifying كل.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Shammākh's verse gives another poetic example of a ghayr phrase qualifying a noun, rather than forming an exception.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He disallows raising Zayd by ellipsis here, since the noun completed by the phrase cannot be left unexpressed in this analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He argues that deleting the noun رجل from لو كان معنا رجل إلا زيد makes the intended exception impossible, so إلا زيد here functions descriptively.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He adduces 21:22 as a parallel in which إلا الله is understood adjectivally, like non-exceptive ghayr. | mentions 21:22
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dhu al-Rumma's line uses إلا بغامها descriptively in place of غير بغامها, demonstrating a non-exceptive use of إلا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He cites 4:95, غير أولي الضرر, as another Quranic example of ghayr used as an adjective. | mentions 4:95
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Labīd's phrase غير الجمل supplies a poetic example of ghayr used descriptively to mean other than the camel.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In another Labīd line, the second ghayr is an adjective for the first; the intended point is that events cannot alter the sharp sword.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After ما أتاني أحد, Sībawayh permits إلا زيد to be parsed either as an appositive or as an adjective.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلوكانمعنارجلإلازيدلغلبنا|والدليلعلىأنهوصفأنك#387/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Without an antecedent noun, ما أتاني إلا زيد cannot be treated like the preceding construction; only the descriptive analysis is available.
[FARRA:v1p4/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The two pronunciations of the pronoun in ʿalayhim are both Arabic dialects.
[FARRA:v1p4/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | With ḍamma on the hāʾ, its original vowel is retained across nominative, accusative, and genitive forms.
[FARRA:v1p4/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | With kasra on the hāʾ, speakers ease the ḍamma after a silent yāʾ; the same two options occur after a preceding kasra, as in bihim.
[FARRA:v1p4/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | After a yāʾ that has become a pronounced alif because its preceding vowel is fatḥa, the pronoun takes only ḍamma.
[FARRA:v1p7/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Genitive ghayri is an adjective of alladhīna, not of the pronoun in ʿalayhim; its definite annexation permits this description because neither expression denotes a specified person.
[FARRA:v1p7/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Ghayri can be accusative as a detached description of ʿalayhim, or genitive after repeating ṣirāṭ as “the path of those other than …”.
[FARRA:v1p7/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, ghayr means lā, so lā is repeated; if ghayr meant “other than,” repeating lā would be ungrammatical.
[FARRA:v1p7/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | rejects | Farra rejects the claim that ghayr in al-ḥamd means “other than” and lā is extra; extra lā requires a preceding negation.
[FARRA:v1p7/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | rejects | The verse “in a well without ḥawr” does not prove an extra lā: here lā is a true negation, while poetry allows an extra lā after an earlier negation.
[FARRA:v1p7/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | In the cited phrase “a well that returns nothing,” ḥāra means that the action leaves no perceptible trace, like grinding that produces no result.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-ṣirāṭ means a road or clear, straight way; an unattributed line uses the phrase ṣirāṭ al-qāṣid.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r10] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Abū Khirāsh’s verse supplies a further example of lā continuing a negative coordination in ولا البكر.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Jarīr’s verse describes the Commander of the Faithful as being on a ṣirāṭ that stays straight even when routes bend.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Mawārid means roads or places one reaches for water, and also villages; the following verse uses ṣirāṭ as a road comparison.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | In ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, the first lā is an extra particle completing the phrase, effectively ‘and the straying.’
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r5] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-ʿAjjāj’s phrase fī biʾr lā ḥawr has an extra lā; the intended sense is a well of ruin or destruction.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Abū al-Najm’s ألا تسخرا means أن يسخرن, showing an extra lā; al-qafandar means ugly and repulsive.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | In the cited line, ‘they reproach me in amusement ألا أحبه’ means ‘that I love it,’ with lā treated as extra.
[MAJAZ:v1p24/r9] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, lā reinforces the preceding negation; Arabic likewise says ‘without good or blessing’ and ‘no benefit nor defense.’
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p37#2/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · النبي | reports | The Prophet points to Jews as those under divine anger, in response to a question at Wādī al-Qurā.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p37#2/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · النبي | reports | The Prophet identifies Christians as the astray when asked who they are at Wādī al-Qurā.
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim is accusative as an appositive to al-ṣirāṭ.
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The alif in anʿamta is hamzat qaṭʿ because its imperfect is yanʿimu, with a ḍamma on the yāʾ.
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Ghayr al-maghḍūbi can be an adjective for those blessed, though ghayr and mithl are ordinarily used with indefinites and can modify definite forms that carry an indefinite sense.
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | prefers | Apposition is better than the adjective analysis because alladhī and alladhīna remain definite; he argues that rajul mithluka is generic, while Zayd mithluka only works as apposition.
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r7] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | prefers | Ṣirāṭ has both sīn and ṣād forms; al-Akhfash prefers ṣād because that is how it is written throughout the Qurʾān.
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r8] AKHFASH, d. 215 · العرب | reports | Arab usage can put al-jammāʾ al-ghafīr in the accusative despite its article, treating it like an indefinite expression.
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · قوم | reports | Some readers construe ghayr al-maghḍūbi as an exception outside the initial statement.
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · أهل الحجاز | reports | In the Hijaz dialect, an exception outside the initial statement after negation is accusative, as in mā fīhā aḥadun illā ḥimāran.
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · غيرهم | reports | Other Arabs treat the exception as part of the initial statement and put it in the nominative.
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | prefers | A genitive form is explained by analogy to alladhī bi-l-rajul; al-Akhfash finds the adjective analysis weak and apposition better, as in the naṣiya example. | mentions 96:15, 96:16
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Ghayr may alternatively be accusative as a circumstantial expression because it is indefinite while its antecedent is definite.
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r7] AKHFASH, d. 215 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijaz dialect feminizes ṣirāṭ like al-ṭarīq, al-zuqāq, al-sabīl, al-sūq, and al-kalāʾ; Tamīm uses masculine forms, while Asad feminizes al-hudā.

[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p38#5/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Those granted favor on the straight path are the prophets and believers.

[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · النبي | reports | The Prophet praised Abdullah's recitation, telling people who wanted the Quran fresh as revealed to follow Ibn Umm ʿAbd's reading.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · عمر | reports | Umar described Abdullah as a container filled with knowledge, supporting Ibn Qutayba's case for his learning.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · النبي | reports | The Prophet's statement لا صلاة إلا بسورة الحمد supports Fatiha's indispensable place in prayer.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Fatiha is the seven oft-repeated and Mother of the Book, meaning its greatest and earliest part; Mecca is similarly called Mother of Villages because it is oldest. | mentions 3:96
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أهل النظر | reports | The theorists explain that Abdullah did not write Fatiha because compilation guarded against doubt, forgetting, additions, and omissions, while it was short and repeated every prayer and rakʿa.

[TAB:1:7/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The phrase specifies which straight path is meant: the path of those God favored through obedience and worship, including angels, prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and the righteous. | mentions 4:69
[TAB:1:7/r10] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Nābigha's line illustrates omission: saying someone is among the camels of Banū Uqays conveys the omitted noun, a camel.
[TAB:1:7/r11] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Farazdaq's line illustrates omission of “they” after “their collars,” since the possessive phrase already indicates the pronoun.
[TAB:1:7/r12] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The reciters unanimously read ghayr with a genitive ending.
[TAB:1:7/r13] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | On one parsing, ghayr is an adjective of alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a specific proper-name-like definite, so an indefinite adjective can describe it.
[TAB:1:7/r14] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Alternatively, ghayr is genitive by an understood repetition of ṣirāṭ: “the path of those You favored, the path of those not under wrath.”
[TAB:1:7/r15] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The two genitive parses are close in meaning: those favored with true guidance are not under God's wrath or astray; the adjectival parse states this directly.
[TAB:1:7/r16] TAB, d. 310 · author | rejects | Although a grammatical route for reading ghayr in the accusative exists, al-Ṭabarī rejects it as anomalous against the reciters' transmitted consensus.
[TAB:1:7/r17] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The possible accusative parse treats ghayr as a detached adjective of the pronoun in ʿalayhim, which is syntactically governed by anʿamta.
[TAB:1:7/r18] TAB, d. 310 · بعض نحويي البصريين | reports | A Basran grammarian takes the accusative as an exception: ask for the path of the favored, excluding those not favored in religion, by analogy with al-Nābigha's exception.
[TAB:1:7/r19] TAB, d. 310 · نحويو الكوفة | rejects | The Kufans reject the exception analysis: “nor” is a negative conjunction, and Arabic coordinates a negative with a negative, not a negation with an exception.
[TAB:1:7/r2] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God promises to bring those who follow this path steadfastly in obedience to Him and His Messenger into the company of the favored. | mentions 4:69
[TAB:1:7/r20] TAB, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers the unanimously transmitted genitive reading; he accepts either of its two sound grammatical explanations.
[TAB:1:7/r21] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The wrathful are identified with those described in the Qur'an as cursed and punished for disobedience; God also shows the community the way to avoid their fate. | mentions 5:60
[TAB:1:7/r22] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In reports from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies the wrathful as the Jews.
[TAB:1:7/r23] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | At the siege of Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet answers a man's question by identifying the besieged Jews as the wrathful.
[TAB:1:7/r24] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, identifies the wrathful as Jews whom God has angered.
[TAB:1:7/r25] TAB, d. 310 · أبو مالك، أبو صالح، ابن عباس، مرة الهمداني، ابن مسعود، وناس من أصحاب النبي | reports | A report collected by al-Suddī from several early authorities identifies the wrathful as the Jews.

[TAB:1:7/r29] TAB, d. 310 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد | reports | ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd identifies the wrathful as the Jews.
[TAB:1:7/r3] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, identifies the favored as obedient worshippers among the angels, prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous.
[TAB:1:7/r30] TAB, d. 310 · زيد | reports | Zayd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd's father, identifies the wrathful as the Jews.
[TAB:1:7/r31] TAB, d. 310 · بعضهم | reports | One view explains God's anger as His imposing punishment on those He is angry with, in this world or the next. | mentions 43:55, 5:60

[TAB:1:7/r33] TAB, d. 310 · بعضهم | reports | A third view affirms an intelligible divine attribute called anger, while distinguishing it from human agitation and affirming that God's essence is free of affliction.
[TAB:1:7/r34] TAB, d. 310 · بعض أهل البصرة | reports | Some Basrans call lā before “the astray” an added particle that completes the expression but contributes no negation, citing poetry and “what prevented you from not prostrating?” | mentions 7:12
[TAB:1:7/r35] TAB, d. 310 · نحويو الكوفة | rejects | Kufan grammarians reject an unmotivated added lā at the start of a phrase and reject coordinating it with ghayr if ghayr means “other than” or an exception.

[TAB:1:7/r47] TAB, d. 310 · زيد | reports | Zayd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd's father, identifies the astray as the Christians.
[TAB:1:7/r48] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | In Arabic, anyone who departs from the intended route and follows an unsound way is astray; Christians receive this label for missing the truth and taking a wrong religious path.
[TAB:1:7/r49] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits.
[TAB:1:7/r5] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report through Ibn Jurayj, identifies the favored as believers.
[TAB:1:7/r50] TAB, d. 310 · بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية | reports | Some ignorant Qadarites infer from calling Christians astray, without calling them those who mislead, that God has no causal role in their acts of misguidance.
[TAB:1:7/r51] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic can attribute an act to its immediate agent or to its cause; the Qur'an says ships “ran” although another causes their motion, so attributing error to Christians does not exclude divine causation. | mentions 10:22
[TAB:1:7/r52] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qur'an explicitly says God guides and misguides, including that He misled the one who made desire his god; this refutes the Qadarite inference. | mentions 45:23
[TAB:1:7/r53] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Human beings acquire their acts through their own power and choice, while God creates the acts' actual existence and brings them into being.
[TAB:1:7/r54] TAB, d. 310 · أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن | reports | Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
[TAB:1:7/r55] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.
[TAB:1:7/r56] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.
[TAB:1:7/r57] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.
[TAB:1:7/r58] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.
[TAB:1:7/r59] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.
[TAB:1:7/r6] TAB, d. 310 · وكيع | reports | Wakīʿ identifies the favored as Muslims.
[TAB:1:7/r60] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.
[TAB:1:7/r61] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.
[TAB:1:7/r62] TAB, d. 310 · أبو هريرة | reports | A second Abū Hurayra version gives the same recitation exchange but is not attributed to the Prophet.
[TAB:1:7/r63] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.
[TAB:1:7/r7] TAB, d. 310 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد | reports | ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says the favored are the Prophet and those with him.
[TAB:1:7/r8] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Obedience and guidance come to the obedient only through God's favor and enabling; the verse attributes their guidance, worship, and obedience to His beneficence.
[TAB:1:7/r9] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The verse leaves the blessing unstated because the nearby phrase already makes clear that the blessing is guidance to the upright path; Arabic can omit what context supplies.
[TAB-FULL:v1p176#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The phrase those You favored explains which straight path is meant: the way of angels, prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous who obey and worship God, as in the promise of Qur'an 4:67–69. | mentions 4:67, 4:68, 4:69
[TAB-FULL:v1p176#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The requested guidance is to the path God described; whoever follows it obediently will be brought to the company and dwelling of those favored, and God never breaks His promise. | mentions 4:69
[TAB-FULL:v1p176#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says those favored include obedient worshippers among angels, prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous.
[TAB-FULL:v1p176#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ربيع | reports | Rabīʿ interprets those favored as the prophets.
[TAB-FULL:v1p176#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas interprets those favored as believers.
[TAB-FULL:v1p176#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · وكيع | reports | Wakīʿ gives the gloss Muslims.
[TAB-FULL:v1p178/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد | reports | ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says those favored are Muhammad and those with him.
[TAB-FULL:v1p178/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verse clearly shows that obedience is attained only through God's favor and enabling, since the verse attributes their guidance, obedience, and worship to His blessing.
[TAB-FULL:v1p178/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The wording omits the explicit object of bestowed favor because the preceding request and the adjacent phrase identifying the straight path make that favor—the upright path—clear; Arabic likewise omits words recoverable from context, as in lines by al-Nābigha and al-Farazdaq.
[TAB-FULL:v1p180#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The first genitive parse makes ghayr an adjective for alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a fully specified proper name but indefinite-like, so it can take this adjective.
[TAB-FULL:v1p180#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The second genitive analysis treats alladhīna as a fully specified definite phrase and supplies a repeated ṣirāṭ: the path of those favored, the path of those outside the objects of wrath.
[TAB-FULL:v1p180#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The two genitive parses have nearly the same implication: those truly favored with guidance to the true religion are not under God's anger and are not astray.
[TAB-FULL:v1p180/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Farazdaq's line omits the pronoun hum, recoverable from the preceding word; similarly, the nearby wording those You favored suffices without restating the understood favor or path.
[TAB-FULL:v1p182/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Even if ghayr repeats ṣirāṭ rather than qualifying those favored, their evident description as guided by God already implies they are neither objects of His anger nor astray.
[TAB-FULL:v1p182/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | An accusative reading of ghayr is grammatically possible but al-Ṭabarī dislikes it because it departs from the established, widely transmitted reading; it would qualify the object pronoun in عليهم and mean not objects of anger or misguidance.
[TAB-FULL:v1p182/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي البصريين | reports | One Basran grammarian takes accusative ghayr as an exception from those favored: exclude those not favored or guided, and do not make us among them.
[TAB-FULL:v1p183/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي البصريين | reports | The Basran exception analysis appeals to al-Nābigha's poem, where the awārī are excepted although they are plainly not part of the preceding group of people.
[TAB-FULL:v1p183/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويو الكوفيين | rejects | Kufan grammarians reject exception: coordinating the negative wa-lā al-ḍāllīn with an exception is unattested, since Arabic coordinates exception with exception and negation with negation.
[TAB-FULL:v1p183/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | He prefers the universally transmitted genitive reading, taking ghayr as an adjective of those favored or as repeated ṣirāṭ; either parse is sound, and he explains the grammatical alternatives because they produce different interpretations.
[TAB-FULL:v1p183/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Those under anger are the p

eople God describes as cursed and punished in Qur'an 5:60; He informs believers of their fate and shows them the route to salvation out of mercy. | mentions 5:60
[TAB-FULL:v1p188/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم | reports | The Prophet identifies those under wrath as the Jews in reports transmitted from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.
[TAB-FULL:v1p188/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق | reports | Reports from the Prophet at the siege of Wādī al-Qurā identify the besieged people under wrath as Jews.
[TAB-FULL:v1p188/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses those under wrath as Jews whom God has been angry with.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي عن أبي مالك وأبي صالح عن ابن عباس ومرة الهمداني عن ابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي | reports | The report attributed through al-Suddī to these early authorities identifies those under wrath as Jews.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid identifies those under wrath as Jews.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ربيع | reports | Rabīʿ says those under wrath are the Jews.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas likewise identifies them as Jews.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says those under wrath are the Jews; he also transmits the same identification from his father.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعضهم | reports | One theological account says God's anger is the imposition of punishment in this life or the next, citing the drowning of Pharaoh's people and the punishment described in Qur'an 5:60. | mentions 43:55, 5:60
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعضهم | reports | A second account understands divine anger as blame for their conduct and verbal reproach or insult.
[TAB-FULL:v1p189/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعضهم | reports | A third account treats anger as a real divine attribute, intelligible by affirmation but unlike human anger, which involves agitation, pain, or harm; it is an attribute like knowledge and power without creaturely limitations.
[TAB-FULL:v1p190/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل البصرة | reports | Some Basrans say lā before those astray is an expendable filler, appealing to poetry and to Qur'an 7:12, which they read as meaning What kept you from prostrating. | mentions 7:12
[TAB-FULL:v1p190/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل البصرة | reports | The same Basran analysis takes ghayr as meaning other than, so the favored are those other than the objects of wrath and the astray.
[TAB-FULL:v1p190/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي الكوفة | rejects | A Kufan grammarian rejects ghayr meaning other than because lā cannot coordinate with سوى absent a prior negative; he also rejects starting lā with an omitted-negation sense without previous negation.
[TAB-FULL:v1p192/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحوي من الكوفة | holds | The Kufan answer reads al-ʿAjjāj's lā as genuine negation and explains the other poems' apparent filler lā by the negative earlier in each sentence, as in the line about Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
[TAB-FULL:v1p192/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | He prefers the Kufan analysis: lā cannot begin as an omitted negative or coordinate with other than or an exception; since ghayr can mean exception, negation, or other than, the only valid reading here is negation, making the verse ask to avoid both groups.
[TAB-FULL:v1p192/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The astray are exemplified by Qur'an 5:77's People of the Book who exceed the truth, follow the desires of already astray people, and stray from the path. | mentions 5:77
[TAB-FULL:v1p192/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم | reports | The Prophet identifies those astray as Christians when asked about the verse.
[TAB-FULL:v1p195/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم | reports | The Prophet tells ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim that those astray are Christians; further routes repeat this identification.
[TAB-FULL:v1p195/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق | reports | Reports from a questioner during the siege at Wādī al-Qurā have the Prophet identify the people asked about as Christians, the astray.
[TAB-FULL:v1p195/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid identifies those astray as Christians.
[TAB-FULL:v1p195/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment.
[TAB-FULL:v1p197/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس والسدي عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي وربيع وعبد الرحمن بن زيد وأبوه | reports | The cited authorities—through Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī's report, Rabīʿ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd and his father—identify those astray as Christians.
[TAB-FULL:v1p197/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one.
[TAB-FULL:v1p197/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Both Jews and Christians are astray and under wrath, but God labels each by a true, recognizable characteristic, without listing every blameworthy trait of either group.
[TAB-FULL:v1p197/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية | reports | Some Qadariyyah wrongly infer from calling Christians astray and Jews objects of wrath that human acts belong only to people and that God does not cause their misguidance; al-Ṭabarī says this betrays ignorance of Arabic attribution and the many verses naming God as guide and misguider. | mentions 10:22, 45:23
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Arabic attributes an act sometimes to its immediate agent and sometimes to its cause: although God creates an act, it is properly attributed to the person who acquires it by power and choice and to God as its creator; Qur'an 10:22 illustrates attribution of sailing to ships though another causes their motion, and 45:23 calls God the guide and misguider. | mentions 10:22, 45:23
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Answering why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses if two contain its meanings: earlier scriptures each included only some meanings, while the Qur'an gathers all of them for Muhammad's community and adds many more.
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The Torah is admonition and detailed instruction, Psalms praise and glorification, and Gospel admonition and reminder, but none has a miracle proving its recipient; the Qur'an contains these meanings and more.
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Among the Qur'an's distinctive merits is its miraculous arrangement and composition: rhetoricians cannot compose even a sura as short as one of its chapters.
[TAB-FULL:v1p203/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa’s extended, distinctive form and combined praise, commands, warnings, stories, arguments, and examples establish Muhammad’s prophethood and teach God’s greatness, blessings, dependence on Him, and fear of disobedience.
[TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو هريرة عن رسول الله | reports | The Prophet reports God praises the servant’s recitation of praise, mercy, and sovereignty, then says the invocation from You alone we worship through the end belongs to the servant. | mentions 1:2, 1:1, 1:4, 1:5
[ZAJJAJ:v1p49/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The phrase is an adjective for al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm. | mentions 1:6
[ZAJJAJ:v1p49/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may carry ḍamma or kasra, the two forms used by most readers; a form with an added wāw is also possible.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p49/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · سِيبَوَيْهِ | reports | Sībawayh says the wāw added after masculine hāʾ parallels the added alif in feminine hāʾ forms.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p49/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · أصحاب سيبويه والخليل | reports | Sībawayh's and al-Khalīl's associates explain the added wāw as clarifying the faint hāʾ; it disappears in pause and is not retained as an original letter.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p49/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | With a preceding kasra the wāw may change to yāʾ; the Hijazi readings of 28:81 include both hī and hū forms. | mentions 28:81
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Some Arabs are reported to use a kasra with the second-person kāf in ʿalaykum and bikum, but he rejects this as an anomalous dialect; the correct poetic wording is faḍl aḥlāmikum.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Sībawayh quotes the poem with the anomalous form, though its sound transmission is faḍl aḥlāmikum.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Plural hāʾ forms originally had a wāw, but speakers omit it because mīm suffices and the wāw is heavy; Arabic names do not end in wāw preceded by a vowel.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | The reading with the wāw in ʿalayhumū is rare; he says the widespread form without it should be read.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | With genitive ghayr, one analysis makes it a substitute for alladhīna, yielding “the path of those other than the angered.”
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Alternatively, genitive ghayr qualifies alladhīna; although ghayr usually describes an indefinite noun, alladhīna here denotes a category rather than particular people.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Accusative ghayr can be an exception, equivalent to “except the angered”; exception ghayr is accusative when what follows illā is accusative.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p52/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Accusative ghayr can instead be a circumstantial, meaning the path of those blessed, not angered.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed

[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | One cannot say mithla ḍārib in the parallel construction, because Zayd depends on ḍārib and cannot precede it.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | After praise and supplication, Arabs use both Amīn and Āmīn; two poems attest the forms.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | An unnamed poet uses Amīn in a prayer that God increase the distance between the speaker and Fataḥl.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Another unnamed poet uses Āmīnā in a prayer for God's mercy on one who says it.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Amīn and Āmīn mean “O God, answer”; they stand in place of a verbal noun for response, like ṣah standing for silence.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p53/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Both are normally paused sounds rather than verb-derived forms; nūn is opened to resolve adjacent quiescent letters, since kasra is heavy after yāʾ, as in ayna and kayfa.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p104/r5] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · ابن كثير وأبو عمرو | reports | The sīn reading of الصراط is transmitted from Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr through named reciters, while Ibn Kathīr also has transmissions with ṣād; Abū ʿAmr is reported with all three sibilant realizations.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p106/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · عريان بن أبي سفيان عن أبي عمرو | reports | One transmission from Abū ʿAmr places the sound between ṣād and zāy; the ordinary reading preserves clear ṣād, while Ḥamza’s imāla approaches zāy and cannot be represented precisely in writing.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p106/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · الكسائي عن حمزة | reports | Reports differ on whether Ḥamza shades only quiescent ṣād toward zāy or also moving ṣād; some say he gives the zāy outright only when ṣād is quiescent.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p106/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī follows Ḥamza in ṣād before dāl in قصد and related forms; he says sīn is more common in Arabic but reads ṣād to follow the written Qurʾānic text. | mentions 16:9, 28:23, 6:46, 52:37, 88:22
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p106/r4] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Sīn is etymologically original, but scribes and readers use ṣād to ease articulation beside emphatic ṭāʾ: both sounds can be made with the tongue raised, unlike sīn and ṭāʾ together.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p108#2/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr connects plural mīm to wāw whether the preceding hāʾ is kasra or ḍamma.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p108#2/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · نافع | reports | Nafiʿ has reports allowing raised or quiescent mīm; the author’s own recitation uses sukūn. Warsh keeps hāʾ kasra and joins mīm to wāw before an initial vowel. | mentions 2:6
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p108#2/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · عاصم ونافع وابن كثير وابن عامر | reports | With a following consonant, these readers keep hāʾ kasra and raise mīm; Abū ʿAmr raises neither, while Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī raise both. | mentions 2:61, 28:23
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p108#2/r4] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Kasra on hāʾ follows a preceding kasra or yāʾ because hāʾ is close to yāʾ; plural wāw is retained as the original plural marker, parallel to dual alif in عليهما.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p108/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Shading ṣād toward voiced zāy matches the voicing of ṭāʾ while retaining a sibilant; the same voicing rationale applies to the cited ṣād+dāl words. | mentions 16:9, 28:23, 6:46
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p108/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza pronounces hāʾ with ḍamma and mīm quiescent in عليهم, إليهم, and لديهم; other readers use kasra on hāʾ.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p110/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · عاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والكسائي | reports | These readers keep hāʾ kasra and mīm sukūn; the dual alif already distinguishes two, while plural mīm distinguishes many, so wāw can be omitted for ease.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p110/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · حمزة | holds | Ḥamza’s ḍamma on hāʾ reflects its underlying form, since the pronoun begins with ḍamma in هم.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p110/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | When mīm meets a following consonant it must move; some restore its original ḍamma while leaving hāʾ kasra, others match kasras to avoid a heavy ḍamma after kasra.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p110/r4] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī restores both mīm and hāʾ to ḍamma before a following consonant, avoiding the transition from kasra to ḍamma.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p110/r5] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · حمزة | holds | Ḥamza limits hāʾ-ḍamma to عليهم, إليهم, and لديهم: when followed by an overt noun, their yāʾ becomes alif, which cannot follow a kasra, so the pronoun follows the overt form. | mentions 8:16, 6:1, 2:142
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p111/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي | reports | These readers take غير المغضوب عليهم in the genitive as an adjective of الذين; Ibn Kathīr is reported with a different form, though another transmission agrees with the majority.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p111/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · الخليل بن أحمد | reports | Al-Khalīl permits Ibn Kathīr’s form as a detached adjective or as an accusative circumstantial phrase; he also allows repeating صراط before غير.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p111/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · الأخفش | rejects | Al-Akhfash analyzes the accusative as an exception, but Ibn Mujāhid explicitly calls this mistaken; genitive غير is the adjective of الذين.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses the path of those favored as the way of those whom God favored.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas identifies those favored as obedient angels, prophets, truthful ones, and martyrs who worshipped God.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid identifies those favored as the believers.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the author says exegetes do not disagree on this wording.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · author | holds | The author says he knows no disagreement among exegetes over the identification of those astray as Christians and those under wrath as Jews.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A second report from the Prophet likewise says the Jews incurred wrath and the Christians went astray.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses the clause as avoiding the way of wrongdoers, especially Christians misled by their claims about God; he prays for the true religion and protection from the punishments of Jews and Christians through divine mercy.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p31/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · author | holds | The author again says he knows no exegetical disagreement over this wording.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Anʿamta ʿalayhim is the relative clause, and its pronoun refers back to alladhīna.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن أبي إسحاق | reports | Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads ʿalayhimu with a ḍamma and retained wāw, the original form.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reads ʿalayhimī with kasra and a retained yāʾ, avoiding yāʾ next to ḍamma and changing wāw after kasra.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أهل المدينة | reports | The people of Medina read ʿalayhim with kasra on hāʾ and a still mīm, a Najdi dialect.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · حمزة وأهل الكوفة | reports | Ḥamza and the Kufans read ʿalayhum with ḍamma on hāʾ and still mīm, dropping the heavy wāw.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الأعرج | reports | Al-Aʿraj reads ʿalayhimu with kasra on hāʾ and a retained wāw.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · محمد بن يزيد | reports | Muḥammad ibn Yazīd rejects as impermissible two irregular forms with hāʾ and mīm both ḍamma or both kasra without wāw or yāʾ.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو العباس | reports | Abū al-ʿAbbās says the kasra in minhu is possible because the nūn is still; Banū Bakr also use kasra in ʿalaykum, but he rejects the analogy as a grave error.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysān permits ghayr al-maghḍūbi as an adjective or apposition to alladhīna, and also as apposition to their pronoun in ʿalayhim.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · عبد الله بن كثير | reports | A report from al-Khalīl says ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr read ghayra al-maghḍūbi in the accusative.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r20] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash parses the accusative as a circumstantial accusative or an exception.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r21] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو العباس | reports | Abū al-ʿAbbās calls it a detached exception rather than an exception from the preceding expression.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r22] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans deny an exception parse because lā follows and, they say, lā is not superfluous in exceptions.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r23] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | The Kufan objection is not binding because lā here carries a negative sense.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r24] NAHHAS, d. 338 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysān says al-maghḍūb is singular in form but plural in sense, like passive participles with a genitive complement.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r25] NAHHAS, d. 338 · البصريون | reports | Basrans treat lā as extra; the Kufans understand it as ghayr.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r26] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; the Kufans call this coordination, while Sībawayh calls it sharing.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r27] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أيوب السختياني | reports | The underlying form al-ḍāllīn is al-ḍāllilīn, with assimilated lām; Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī read the lām with hamza.
[NAHHAS:v1p174/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ is an appositional substitute, and alladhīna is genitive by annexation and indeclinable so its middle does not inflect.
[IBNHIBBAN:1797/r1] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · أبو هريرة | rep

orts | Nuaim reports that Abu Hurayra began with the basmala, recited the Fatiha, said amin at its end with the congregation, and performed the prayer actions before saying his prayer most resembled the Prophet's.
[IBNHIBBAN:1804/r1] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet instructs worshippers to say amin when the imam reaches the verse's ending; the imam and angels say it too, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins.
[IBNHIBBAN:1804/r2] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · أبو حاتم | holds | Abu Hatim explains that matching the angels means saying amin sincerely for God, free of vanity, showing off, or desire for reputation, as the angels do.
[IBNHIBBAN:1805/r1] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · وائل بن حجر | reports | Wail ibn Hujr reports that while praying with the Prophet, he heard him say amin after reciting ‘nor those astray.’
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p62#2/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The sīn form preserves the word’s original consonant; ṣād replaces sīn to harmonize its hissing quality with ṭāʾ’s emphatic articulation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p57/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Ḥamza alone uses a damma on the hāʾ and a still mim in ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim; the others use a kasra on hāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p57/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr joins the plural mim to a wāw after either a kasra or damma on hāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p57/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · إسماعيل بن جعفر وابن جماز وقالون والمسيبي | reports | Some Nāfiʿ transmitters allow either a damma or still mim after kasra hāʾ; Aḥmad b. Qālūn infers Nāfiʿ read with still mim, as did Aḥmad b. Mūsā.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p57/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ورش | reports | Warsh keeps hāʾ kasra and mim still, but inserts a wāw when an original alif follows, as in sawāʾ ʿalayhumu.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p57/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī generally use kasra hāʾ and still mim; before a following sukūn, readers differ over mim and sometimes hāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p57/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أحمد بن موسى | holds | Aḥmad b. Mūsā says the variation of hāʾ depends on whether it follows kasra or silent yāʾ; elsewhere it is damma, while mim is damma or still.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh reports that some say ʿalayhumu by assimilating to the preceding yāʾ; Abū Ḥātim identifies it as al-Aʿraj’s reading.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | One defense says hāʾ shares yāʾ’s articulation, so the hāʾ should follow the yāʾ; another treats hāʾ as related to yāʾ by its articulation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عاصم وأبو عمرو والكسائي وابن عامر | reports | Their kasra-hāʾ, still-mim reading deletes wāw because the plural mim itself prevents confusion with the dual, and deletion lightens speech.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عاصم وأبو عمرو والكسائي وابن عامر | reports | They preserve kasra on hāʾ because it is the same pronoun hāʾ as in ʿalayhi and its cause for kasra remains unchanged after mim is added.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza treats damma hāʾ as original, like hum when independent; the waw reading is described as old and Qurayshī, Ḥijāzī, and Yemeni eloquent usage.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza limits damma to these three forms because before a visible noun, ʿalā, ladā, and ilā end in alif and hāʾ is not kasra after alif.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو حاتم | reports | Damma on a mim before a following sukūn restores its original vowel after movement becomes necessary; this is common in the two Holy Cities.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p59/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Kasra mim before a following sukūn assimilates kasra to kasra, avoiding the heaviness of damma after kasra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p61/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī keeps hāʾ kasra unless the mim meets a following sukūn, then restores both hāʾ and mim to damma to avoid switching from kasra to damma.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p61/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | prefers | The author prefers kasra on hāʾ because it is easier to pronounce and is the majority reading.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p61/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh explains kasra hāʾ after yāʾ or kasra by its hidden quality and closeness to yāʾ and alif; adjacent kasra also changes wāw to yāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p61/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | When the next word begins with sukūn, kasra mim is preferred as lighter; it restores an original vowel, and Ḥasan’s alayhimi preserves the connecting yāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p63/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Abū ʿAlī argues that hāʾ resembles alif in articulation and hiddenness, so a preceding kasra or yāʾ draws its damma toward kasra as imāla draws alif toward yāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p63/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The pronunciation ḍarabtu ḍarbih shows hāʾ can trigger imāla even without a preceding kasra or yāʾ, like imāla in some proper names.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p63/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Hāʾ and alif both clarify a preceding vowel in pause; al-Khalīl permits either hāʾ or alif after a consonant, supporting their parallel treatment in ʿalayhim.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p63/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The optional hāʾ or alif suffix is allowed because each resembles and can stand for the other; alif also occurs in the same pause pattern after bāʾ, tāʾ, and thāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p63/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Although hāʾ lacks the sustained sound of alif, their shared hiddenness, weakness, and articulation allow one to be brought near the other.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p64/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Hāʾ can replace other letters in pause just as alif can, another sign of their similarity.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p64/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Pronoun hāʾ’s hiddenness is shown by movements inserted before it in pause, and by their disappearance in liaison when hāʾ itself makes the vowel clear.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p64/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | rejects | The reported phrase lam aḍribihimā is treated as liaison pronounced like pause, not as a general rule for inflectional sukūn; inflectional endings do not assimilate freely.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p64/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | A jussive consonant may move to avoid a following sukūn, as in the cited yattaqihi form, unlike a freely altered inflectional ending.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p67/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The phrase اشتر لنا سويقا can be explained by treating the liaison as pause, among the analyses of movement before pronoun hāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p67/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Hāʾ behaves like weak letters: it can be deleted word-finally, as in shāh, shafah, and sanah, and shared rules strengthen the analogy.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p67/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Hāʾ substitutes for yāʾ in ذه/هذه; Ḥijāzī and Tamīmī dialects differ in whether it drops or becomes yāʾ in pause and liaison.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p67/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Hāʾ also alternates with yāʾ under doubling, as in dahdayt for dahdaht and related forms.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p67/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd records the forms māhat and tamūhu/tamīhu, and a poetic line using māh as a word for a heart softened by tears.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p67/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Some speakers kasra hāʾ despite an intervening consonant, as in minhum; this weaker analogy still supports kasra when yāʾ is adjacent.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p69/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd reports a Bakrī speaker saying minhu, minhuma, and minhumī, breaking the pronoun in both connected and paused speech.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p69/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Other Bakrī speakers say bikum and faḍlu aḥlāmikum with kasra on kāf, since kāf shares hāʾ’s whispering and pronoun function.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p69/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The attachment of weak vowels to kāf and hāʾ further supports kasra in ʿalayhim because hāʾ has many similar features.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p69/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | reports | An objection says damma is the default for genitive pronoun hāʾ, as its accusative counterpart is damma and damma works in more environments than kasra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p69/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | rejects | The author replies that proximity can override a default vowel; Arabic regularly abandons original sounds for harmony or ease, including ṣād in ṣirāṭ and several broken forms.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p71/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Numerous forms depart from their expected morphology: ʿīd has plural aʿyād, dunya’s pattern is otherwise abandoned, and Adam/Akhir form plurals with wāw despite an expected hamza.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p71/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The expected form of qasī is abandoned in three respects, illustrating that a linguistic default need not prevail when analogy or ease favors another form.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p71/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Hamza’s reading in buyūt shows that kasra can replace a default damma because of nearby yāʾ; Sibawayh’s diminutive bayyit supports the same allowance.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p71/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Because diminutive and broken plural formation are analogous processes, adjacent kasra may replace damma in a plural; this supports kasra in ʿalayhim for harmony and ease.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p73/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Poetic rhyme treats moving hāʾ as a connective following the rhyme, like silent alif, wāw, and yāʾ; named examples include al-Aʿshā’s verse.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p73/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The hāʾ in bihi and ʿalayhi can th

[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p73/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | A moving hāʾ is often ignored as a separator: imāla occurs before it in yadribahā, yanziʿahā, and baynī wa-baynahā, as before alif.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p73/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The shared opening of the doubled dāl in raddahā and raddā likewise shows that hāʾ does not block the alif-like pattern.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p73/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | These analogies lead to the reading that deletes the weak glide after the plural mim rather than counting moving hāʾ as a separator.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p76/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | When moving hāʾ is not counted, retaining its following yāʾ or wāw would leave two adjacent sukūns; deletion is therefore favored in fīhi hudan and khudhūhu.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p76/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Weak letters are deleted in many settings where other letters remain, including suffixes, possessive forms, pauses, and rhyme, so deleting the glide after mim is ordinary.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p76/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Poetic examples demonstrate deletion of weak endings in verse and rhyme; the text also reports a variant wording for the line with sawāfa.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p76/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Deleting waw or yāʾ after ʿalayhim is light and unambiguous because these suffixes are often dropped, even when nothing remains to mark them.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p76/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Repeated deletion of weak endings makes it legitimate to apply the same deletion to nouns as well as other forms.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p78/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Final alif is retained in pauses and rhyme while yāʾ may be deleted; exceptional deletion of alif is poetic necessity, so it does not refute the rule.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p78/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Since plural mim can take alif, wāw, or yāʾ and alif is not deleted, loss of wāw or yāʾ creates no ambiguity.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p78/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Both lexical and grammatical weak endings are deleted elsewhere, even without a surviving marker; that makes deletion from ʿalayhim especially fitting.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p78/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Retaining the mim vowel could restore the missing glide through vowel lengthening, so a still mim best realizes the intended lightening.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p80/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | A kasra or damma may be lengthened into the very yāʾ or wāw that was deleted; still mim prevents that reversal and preserves the lighter form.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p80/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Plural mim always follows a kasra or damma, both heavy, unlike singular pronoun hāʾ, which can follow fatha or sukūn; this licenses still mim.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p80/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The shared deletion in pause follows naturally because plural glide deletion already occurs in liaison, and pause permits still more changes.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p82/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | A vowelled mim would create four or five consecutive moving syllables, a sequence avoided in Arabic word patterns and poetic meters; deleting its vowel prevents that sequence.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p82/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Arabic meter alternates deletions in mustafʿilun to avoid five consecutive movements, an analogy for removing mim’s vowel.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p82/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | reports | Ḥamza’s damma reading treats the derived yāʾ as nonessential, like alif, so hāʾ takes damma as it does after alif; forms ʿalāk and ilāk support this.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p84/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Arabic alternations such as ḥāḥayt, ṭāʾī, and ḥārī support the close relation of yāʾ and alif; alif from wāw is comparatively rare.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p84/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Against the claim that dāwiya has an alif derived from wāw, Abū ʿAlī suggests it may derive from daw with a nisba ending, supported by a cited poetic use.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p84/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The common analogy should prevail over a rare alternative unless evidence forces the exception; poetic shortening of nisba yāʾ does not do so.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p84/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd reports an eloquent Arab saying ḍarabat yadāh and waḍaʿtuhu ʿalāh; al-Khalīl used such speech to explain forms with alif-like treatment.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p87/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p87/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Ḥijāz and Qays use final hāʾ in both pause and liaison, paralleling Ṭayyiʾ’s yāʾ substitution and strengthening the analogy.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p87/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | The attested dialect and the analogous Ḥijāzī/Tamīmī alternations establish the language and make its use for Ḥamza’s reading legitimate.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p87/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | rejects | Replacing alif with wāw is weaker than replacing it with yāʾ because it is less attested and less supported by analogy.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p87/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Poetic meter balances duration, so the longer alif cannot share the rhyme position of yāʾ and wāw.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p89/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Unlike long alif, short fatha can precede a rhyme with damma or kasra; examples from Abū al-Ḥasan show the distinction.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p89/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Alif’s greater duration appears in how hamza is softened after alif but not after yāʾ or wāw, strengthening its distinct treatment.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p89/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Yāʾ and wāw do not assimilate into alif because alif is long and always still; sibilants likewise resist stops because their extra hiss is absent from stops.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p89/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | A derived letter can retain the behavior of its source: yāʾ originating from alif in ʿalayhim is treated as alif, so hāʾ is rounded as after alif.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p91/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Examples such as ruwiya, ruwiyya, and nuwwi show that a replacement wāw can inherit the behavior of its source; bīs similarly keeps its original kasra after hamza is dropped.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p91/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Therefore the yāʾ in ʿalayhim may behave as the alif from which it derives, supporting Ḥamza’s damma on hāʾ.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p91/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Yāʾ can also be fixed across case positions like alif, preserving one surface form; he cites ayādī sabā, bādī badā, qālī qalā, and maʿdīkarib.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p91/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | These fixed-yāʾ forms occur in accusative position, whether analyzed as one of the cited nominal patterns or as an attached ending.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p43/r1] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى | reports | Abū Bakr counts seven transmitted vocalizations of the pronoun in عليهم; al-Akhfash adds three, yielding ten forms, five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with kasra.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p43/r2] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · ابن أبي إسحاق ومسلم بن جندب والأعرج وعيسى الثقفي وعبد الله بن يزيد | reports | These readers transmit عليهمو; al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr b. Fāʾid transmit عليهمي, while al-Aʿraj is also reported with two unextended forms.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p43/r3] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | Ibn Jinnī regards the plural wāw as original: mīm marks more than one, including the dual, while wāw specifically marks the plural.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p43/r4] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | He derives عليهمي from kasra spreading from the preceding yāʾ to the weak, nearby hāʾ, then to mīm; the wāw becomes yāʾ after a kasra.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | The blessed are knowers granted knowledge, saints granted sincerity, contentment, and certainty, the righteous granted patience and compassion, seekers granted obedience's sweetness, and believers granted steadfastness.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | The blessed are granted knowledge of God and understanding from Him.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعض البغداديين | reports | The blessed relinquish personal interests and stand with God in good etiquette.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r12] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The blessed witness the Benefactor rather than the gift itself.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r13] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The blessed have outward Islam and inward faith, echoing God's gifts both outwardly and inwardly (31:20). | mentions 31:20
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r14] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | They have cosmic darkness removed from their secrets and spirits purified by holy light, so their aspiration witnesses God alone.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r15] SULAMI, d. 412 · محمد بن علي | reports | God's favor restrains their limbs through awe while they serve Him.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو عثمان | reports | God's favor includes teaching them the path's dangers, Satan's tricks, and the ego's treachery.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · محمد بن الفضل | reports | The blessed path is acceptance of the obligations God imposed.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو الحسن الوراق | reports | Divine care keeps the blessed steadfast on the path of intimate conversation with God.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The blessed were assigned happiness in pre-eternity.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعض البغداديين | reports | God's favor annihilates attention to blessings through the

[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The blessed see what was decreed for them eternally without that disclosure distracting them from God.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · مالك بن أنس | reports | The blessed path means following the Prophet.
[SULAMI:v1p41#2/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The favor consists of faith, guidance, enabling, care, watchfulness, and protection.
[SULAMI:v1p43/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The blessed path comes from God's hidden realm through the lights of His guidance.
[SULAMI:v1p43/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | The path is worshipping God as though one sees Him, as in the Prophetic definition of excellence.
[SULAMI:v1p43/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | The blessed path means following the Sunnah.
[SULAMI:v1p43/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | God's favor includes granting permission to converse with and petition Him.
[SULAMI:v1p43/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan identifies the recipients of favor as Abu Bakr and Umar.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Those under anger are abandoned, expelled, and humiliated; the astray have left God's guidance, knowledge, and guardianship.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | The supplicant asks God to act accordingly and not leave him to himself for even an instant.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر | reports | Amin means heading toward God, who is too generous to refuse one who heads to Him.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r12] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Amin admits incapacity to praise God through one's own attributes except by following Muhammad al-Amin.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r13] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعض العراقيين | reports | Amin expresses hope that God will answer the supplications just made.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r14] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Amin can ask to be spared from one's requests because God's choice is better than one's own.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r15] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Amin means being content with God's decree for and against the servants.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The condemned follow the path of the doomed, while the astray follow desire away from guidance.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Those under anger are consumed in Satan's wastelands; the astray are expelled from obedience to the Merciful.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Anger is associated with seeing one's own acts or seeking compensation for deeds; error is failing to see favors or thank God for enabled service.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Anger follows bad etiquette in service; the contrasting phrase refers to turning back in repentance, though its wording is broken in this segment.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Anger is linked with ostentation, and error with abandoning Sunnah in the pillars of worship.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو عثمان | reports | He associates being under anger with leaving this chapter's recitation in prayer and being astray with not reciting it; the wording is awkward in the source.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Anger means being left to oneself, while error means losing God's protection and attachment.
[SULAMI:v1p44/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Anger follows innovations, while error is abandoning guidance and Sunnah, including the Sunnah of saying Amin aloud after the chapter in prayer.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The phrase is an appositive to the first ṣirāṭ: those favored are guided and cared for in affirmation of divine unity; the author identifies them as prophets and believers and cites 4:69. | mentions 4:69
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · الأعمش | reports | Al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza read ʿalayhum with ḍamma on hāʾ and a still mīm; a report attributes it to the Prophet and ʿUmar as well.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · عيسى بن عمر | reports | ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read with ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm and an added wāw.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr and al-Aʿraj read with kasra on hāʾ, ḍamma on mīm, and an appended wāw.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reads with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm and an appended yāʾ.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās identifies them as the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed God's favors upon them.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · شهر بن حوشب | reports | Shahr ibn Ḥawshab identifies them as the Prophet's companions and his household.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima says they were granted steadfastness in faith and uprightness.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · علي بن الحسين بن داود | reports | ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Dāwūd says they give thanks in ease and patience in hardship.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl understands the favor as God completing His blessing upon them.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Niʿma originally conveys increase or doing something thoroughly; the usage أنعما for Abū Bakr and ʿUmar means they surpassed others in good.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · الصادق | reports | Al-Ṣādiq reads the phrase as ‘the path of those whom You favored’; ʿAmr ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAlī also read it this way, with lām governing the following word.
[THALABI:v1p121#2/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The common reading has ʿalayhim with kasra on hāʾ and a still mīm.
[THALABI:v1p122/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله بن عطاء الخفاف | reports | ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Khaffāf transmits from Abū ʿAmr a kasra on hāʾ and a lightly articulated ḍamma on mīm.
[THALABI:v1p122/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · عمرو بن حامد | reports | ʿAmr ibn Ḥāmid reads the word with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm.
[THALABI:v1p122/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The variants arise from the original ḍamma, neighboring yāʾ favoring kasra, the heaviness of ḍamma beside a still yāʾ, assimilation, easing, and appending wāw or yāʾ for vowel harmony.
[THALABI:v1p122/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Ghayr functions as an adjective for alladhīna despite the usual definiteness mismatch, because alladhīna here is not a fully specified definite but means whoever is truthful rather than lying.
[THALABI:v1p122/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The intended sense is ‘other than the path of those upon whom You were angry.’
[THALABI:v1p123/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | One group explains God's anger as His will to take vengeance on sinners.
[THALABI:v1p123/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | Another explanation calls anger a kind of punishment opposite to divine pleasure.
[THALABI:v1p123/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · قيل | reports | A third explanation defines anger as condemnation of sinners for the ugliness of their acts.
[THALABI:v1p123/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | God's anger does not reach sinful believers; it reaches unbelievers.
[THALABI:v1p123/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The misguided are those who have strayed from guidance; the root suggests loss or disappearance, and a poetic line uses it of a people who lost their way.
[THALABI:v1p123/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’
[THALABI:v1p123/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن كثير | reports | Khalīl ibn Aḥmad transmits Ibn Kathīr's accusative reading of ghayr al-maghḍūb.
[THALABI:v1p123/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar and ʿAlī read ‘and not those astray.’
[THALABI:v1p123/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · السختياني | reports | Al-Sakhtiyānī reads lā al-ḍāllīn with hamza to break the meeting of two unvowelled consonants.
[THALABI:v1p124/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله | reports | In a report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies those angered with the Jews and those astray with the Christians.
[THALABI:v1p124/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله | reports | At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet points to Jews fighting him as those angered and to Christians as the other party, those astray.
[THALABI:v1p124/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author links divine anger against Jews to 5:60 and the description of Christians as astray to 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77
[THALABI:v1p124/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · الواقدي | reports | Al-Wāqidī glosses those angered as people who oppose and disobey, and those astray as people who leave religion and faith.
[THALABI:v1p124/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · التستري | reports | Al-Tustarī identifies innovation with those angered and departure from Sunna with those astray.

[MAWARDI:1:7/r11] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A third interpretation is that God’s wrath means His condemnation of them.
[MAWARDI:1:7/r12] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A fourth interprets wrath as a kind of punishment named anger, just as God’s blessings are named mercy.
[MAWARDI:1:7/r13] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Misguidance is the opposite of guidance.
[MAWARDI:1:7/r14] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | God singles out Jews as the objects of wrath because they are the most hostile.
[MAWARDI:1:7/r15] MAWARDI, d. 450 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Umar ibn al-Khattab reads ghayr before al-dallin as well, repeating ghayr in the phrase.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r17] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One account understands divine anger as the anger known among human beings.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r18] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A second account interprets God's anger as a will to punish; anger linguistically means severity, a quality unsuitable for God.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r19] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third account interprets God's anger as His condemnation of them.
