[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God keeps the seekers from settling among likenesses through the gentle gift of union and disclosure of majesty and beauty.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Another description of the favored is that they fulfill God's rights without turning aside to secure their own interests.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r11] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | They are also described as purified of their own traces so that they reach God through God.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r12] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | They have been freed from Satan's snares, the soul's errors, and imagined arrival before human traces have faded.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r13] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | They rely on God, disown their own power, and witness their prior happiness in God's choice and His unity in what He decrees as pleasant or painful.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r14] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | The favored preserve proper etiquette in service and remain aware of reverent awe.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r15] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | They preserve the rules of sacred law even during overpowering disclosures of spiritual realities, never exceeding knowledge or neglecting a ruling.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r16] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | The suns of their knowledge do not extinguish the lights of their scrupulousness, and they never neglect a rule of the Law.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r17] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | The favored remain servants even when the power of spiritual reality appears.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r18] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Those under wrath are struck by abandonment, deprivation, rejection, separation, and expulsion.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r19] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | They are also described as humiliated and ruined, occupied with pursuing gratification while imagining they possess something; their misery has a divine secret.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Guidance to truth prevents reliance on the means of spiritual practice and keeps conjecture from clouding the oneness of God.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r20] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Another group tasted nearness for a time, then was turned to distance and failed to reach the intimacy it desired; its effort and hope came to nothing.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r21] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Those under wrath forgot divine enabling and closed their eyes to the sight of divine support.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r22] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Those who go astray fail to witness God's prior choice and the unfolding of His decrees.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r23] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Those under wrath also neglect the etiquette of service and fall short in fulfilling the conditions of obedience.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r24] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | They can also be people cut off in the deserts of absence, scattered by worries through valleys of conjecture.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r25] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Saying amin after the Fatiha is Sunnah and means “Lord, do and answer”; it seeks enabling for deeds and fulfillment of hopes through humble petition.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r26] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The strongest means for the needy is continual seeking of God's aid, expressed through sincere supplication and disavowal of one's own power and ability.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | “Guide us” asks God to remove the darkness of one's states and the shadow of one's striving so that His holiness and generosity become lights by which one finds Him.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The straight path keeps Satan's impulses, the soul's notions, inherited imitation, routine instruction, habit, fatigue, weak resolve, and greed from delaying arrival or insight.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The straight path is proved by Scripture and Sunna; innovation has no authority or route upon it.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | It is also the path validated by signs of monotheism, witnesses of realization, the early Muslim community, and lessons drawn from evidence.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The path separates its travelers from self-interest and its seekers from claims to personal entitlement.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The path leads to monotheism and lets its traveler witness divine care and generosity, so effort is not mistaken for a claim that reward is owed.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p13/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Those favored with this path are saints and the elect, whom God has annihilated from themselves and established through Himself, without hidden divine stratagems stopping them.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p530/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ in ṣirāṭ alladhīna is an appositive restating the first ṣirāṭ in meaning, like calling one's father by the name Zayd.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p530/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Relative pronouns such as alladhī and alladhīna are incomplete until their clause supplies a predicate, verb, circumstance, or conditional structure; that clause must contain a pronoun referring back.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p530/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Alladhīna is indeclinable across nominative, accusative, and genitive because it remains incomplete without its relative clause and thus resembles a particle.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p530/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A singular indeclinable relative gains case marking in the dual because particles are not dualized, but the plural is again a single form like hāʾulāʾ and remains indeclinable.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p530/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq, following Sībawayh, al-Khalīl, and al-Akhfash, says the original form of alladhī was ladh on the faʿl pattern.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p530/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الفتح الموصلي | reports | Abū al-Fatḥ al-Mawṣilī says the alif and lām in alladhī and related forms are fixed additions: other relatives such as man, mā, and ayy are definite without them, and the relative clause itself identifies alladhī.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p533/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The added lām is retained because alladhī enables a clause to describe a definite noun: ordinary clauses are indefinite, and the particle alif-lām cannot attach directly to a clause.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p533/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Alladhī turns the sentence into a relative clause and marks the description as definite, as in the construction Zayd alladhī abūhu munṭaliq.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p533/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | In the verse, ṣirāṭ alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim means the road of those on whom You bestowed favor; the clause could describe an indefinite qawm directly, but not a definite group.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p535/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | God's inʿām is His favor and gift; niʿma is a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive inʿām, as nafaqa stands for infāq.

468 · author | holds | The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may be pronounced with either kasra or ḍamma; kasra follows because yāʾ is related to kasra and the lighter transition is preferred.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p535/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says wāw was added after masculine hāʾ just as alif was added after feminine hāʾ, balancing their added endings.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p535/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says wāw was added to make the faint throat-produced hāʾ clearer with a labial long vowel; the connecting wāw drops in pause and changes to yāʾ after kasra.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p535/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Because hāʾ is a weak barrier, the preceding kasra acts as if it directly preceded the added wāw; that explains kasra in ʿalayhi and its retention in ʿalayhim.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السراج | reports | Ibn al-Sarrāj explains the plural mīm's sukūn as lightening: the dual's alif already signals two, while the indispensable plural mīm lets speakers drop wāw without ambiguity.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ورش عن نافع | reports | Warsh from Nāfiʿ pronounces plural mīm with ḍamma and links a following initial hamza with wāw; dropping hamza and moving its vowel requires the mīm to recover its original ḍamma and lengthen.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Warsh lengthens before an open hamza rather than transferring its fatḥa to mīm, which could make the plural resemble the dual; he follows the same pattern before other hamza vowels.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pronounce hāʾ and mīm with ḍamma at a following hamzat al-waṣl: mīm returns to its original vowel to break two sukūns, then hāʾ follows it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr uses kasra for mīm as the usual vowel when breaking two sukūns and also gives hāʾ kasra to avoid a heavy kasra-to-ḍamma transition.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | Readers who keep hāʾ kasra but give mīm ḍamma restore mīm to its original vowel without restoring hāʾ, which was not forced by the context.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p541/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says those given favor were the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed God's blessings.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima says God favored them by keeping them firm in faith and steadfast.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | Another interpretation identifies them with the people in 4:69 who obey God and the Messenger. | mentions 4:69
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · محمد بن جرير | reports | Ibn Jarīr says the verse is elliptical: guide us along the path of those You favored with guidance to the path, since Arabic omits words when context supplies them.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Ghayr can be genitive as an appositive to alladhīna or as its adjective; the adjective is valid because the relative phrase here is not a particular, singled-out group.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Ghayr may instead be accusative as a circumstantial expression or an exception meaning except those under wrath; as a circumstantial phrase it means not those under wrath.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السراج | reports | Ibn al-Sarrāj additionally allows accusative as an implied aʿnī, I mean; al-Khalīl reportedly allowed it as a detached form of praise.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | The author chooses genitive: although ghayr and mithl are usually indefinite even when annexed to a definite word, a known thing with one known opposite makes ghayr definite.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p543/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | If a known thing has one known opposite, ghayr annexed to that opposite is definite, as in movement versus stillness.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | The author of al-Ḥujja says genitive ghayr is either apposition or adjective; apposition implies repeating the governing factor, as the repeated prepositions in 7:75 show. | mentions 7:75
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | Apposition differs from an adjective because an indefinite can replace a definite and an expressed noun can replace a pronoun, neither of which is allowed for modifiers.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | Apposition also repeats the understood governing case factor, while both apposition and adjective clarify the first noun.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | holds | As apposition, ghayr has a clear meaning whether construed definite or indefinite, since both definite and indefinite apposition are accepted.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | As an adjective, ghayr can modify alladhīna here only because the relative phrase does not single out a particular group, making it like an indefinite description.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | A parallel is the definite al-rajul described by mithluka: the article does not identify a particular man, so the description remains nonspecific.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p546/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | In the verse, ghayr al-maghḍūb describes the favored people and is definite because one favored with faith is not under wrath.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p550/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | In 4:95, ghayr can modify the believers sitting out: the intended contrast is healthy nonparticipants versus those who strive. | mentions 4:95
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p550/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | rejects | Al-Farrāʾ rejects accusative ghayr as an exception, arguing that a positive exception cannot be followed by negative lā in coordination.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p550/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | Those allowing exception say an exception resembles negation, so all came except Zayd can mean all came, not Zayd; lā can coordinate by meaning or be an addition.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p550/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | The author concludes al-Farrāʾ's objection has no force, since lā can follow exception under either of those analyses.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p550/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Lā may also be added after ghayr as a circumstantial expression, adjective, or appositive; the Qur'an uses it in 57:29. | mentions 57:29
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p550/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · some grammarians | reports | Some allow added lā only after a preceding negation, but the author rejects that restriction and cites Saʿida al-Hudhalī's affirmative example.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p553/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Before an indefinite, lā may be extra; if not extra, it either joins the noun as one genitive compound or contributes negation without affecting the noun's case.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p553/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Examples of the compound include min lā shayʾ and bi-lā māl; lā plus noun functions as a single expression, like fifteen.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p553/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The non-compounding negator leaves case untouched, as in al-Nābigha's no uncle and al-Shammākh's sleepless night.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p553/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The author of al-Naẓm says lā in wa-lā al-ḍāllīn prevents misreading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those favored; it marks coordination with ghayr, which implies negation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p553/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | He illustrates the disambiguating role with a poem: lā before ʿUmar keeps him inside the Prophet's disapproval clause instead of starting a new sentence praising Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The root of ḍalāl is disappearance: water disappears into milk, and a disbeliever disappears from the path of truth; 32:10 uses the word for bodies lost in earth after death. | mentions 32:10
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Aḍalla can mean to hide or bury something, as in al-Mukhabbal's poem about Banū Qays losing their leader.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Thus the astray person is absent from truth and has deviated from right guidance; the verb has reported variant forms.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عدي بن حاتم | reports | A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · النبي | reports | A second report says the Prophet at Wādī al-Qurā was asked by a man from Bali about two groups; he pointed to Jews as those under wrath and Christians as astray; no grading is stated.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وغيرهم | reports | Commentators support this interpretation by citing God's anger against Jews in 5:60 and the description of people who strayed in 5:77; Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and Mujāhid hold it. | mentions 5:60, 5:77
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | The identification also fits a rare accusative reading of ghayr as exception, excluding Jews and Christians from those favored; the author notes that this reading is anomalous.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | For the standard reading, the sense is the path of those favored who are neither under wrath nor astray; denying these traits implicitly attributes them to others, supporting implication in discourse.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p557/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The Prophet and the exegetes have already identified who are under wrath and who are astra

[WAHIDI-QT:1:7/r2] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · قيل | reports | Another view identifies the favored people with those named in the verse about being with those God favored. | mentions 4:69
[WAHIDI-QT:1:7/r3] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | Those under wrath are Jews; God's wrath means His willing punishment.
[WAHIDI-QT:1:7/r4] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | Those astray are Christians, and Muslims ask to avoid both their error and the Jews' incurred wrath.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Those granted favor are the followers of Moses and Jesus before they changed God's favor.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r5] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · قيل | reports | Another identification is those described as being with the people God favored in 4:69. | mentions 4:69
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r6] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Those under divine anger are the Jews; God's anger means His willing punishment.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r7] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The people who went astray are the Christians; Muslims ask to avoid their deviation from truth as well as the Jews' incurred anger.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p328/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | In al-Fātiḥa, ṣirāṭ is the object, al-mustaqīm its adjective, ṣirāṭ alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim apposes the preceding phrase, and the remaining clauses modify or coordinate with it.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p328/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | rejects | Syntactic relations are not lexical meanings: word order is not itself a word, and inflection cannot be two signs with one serving as the other's explanation.
[DAMGHANI:v1p460/r6] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Niʿmah can mean prophethood, as in the people favored with prophecy. | mentions 4:69, 93:11
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim with ḍamma throughout the Qur’an.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · يعقوب | reports | Yaʿqūb gives ḍamma to each hāʾ preceded by a vowelless yāʾ, including forms such as ʿalayhim and fīhim, and reportedly also where that yāʾ drops.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Readers vary between kasra and ḍamma on the hāʾ, and between a vowelless, kasra, or ḍamma mīm of the plural, especially before a following hamzat al-waṣl; the author lists each school’s distributions.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ḍamma on hāʾ restores its underlying form; kasra is influenced by the preceding yāʾ, avoiding a heavy shift from ḍamma beside yāʾ, while ḍamma on mīm restores its base and appended wāw lengthens it.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Inʿām, iḥsān, and ifḍāl are near-synonyms, though one may act beneficently toward oneself but cannot bless oneself; niʿma derives from softness and denotes good intended benefit.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | God blesses both believers and unbelievers; His first favor to a servant is creating that person alive for benefit.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r1] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | The favored are those on whom God bestowed guidance and enabling grace.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r10] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · يعقوب | reports | Yaʿqub uses ḍamma on each hāʾ preceded by a quiescent yāʾ in dual and plural forms, except in “between their hands and feet.”
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r11] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | Other readers use kasra on the hāʾ, following the preceding quiescent yāʾ, which is the sister of kasra; ḍamma returns to the hāʾ's isolated form.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r12] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · ابن كثير وأبو جعفر | reports | Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar lengthen the plural mīm in connected reading unless a quiescent letter follows, in which case they do not lengthen it.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r13] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · نافع | reports | Nafiʿ allows a choice in the plural mīm's lengthening.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r14] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · ورش | reports | Warsh uses ḍamma before hamzat al-qaṭʿ.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r15] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · حمزة والكسائي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب | reports | Before hamzat al-waṣl, Hamza and al-Kisa'i use ḍamma after kasra or silent yāʾ; Abu ʿAmr uses kasra on both letters, as does Yaʿqub when the preceding letter is kasra.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r16] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | The remaining readers use a ḍamma on mīm and kasra on hāʾ throughout, owing to the yāʾ or preceding kasra and the mīm's original ḍamma.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r17] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r18] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | God's anger does not befall sinful believers; it befalls only disbelievers.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r19] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | The phrase means those who are not astray from guidance; the root of misguidance conveys destruction and disappearance, like water disappearing in milk.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r2] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · عكرمة | reports | Ikrima says they are the prophets, whom God kept firm in faith and uprightness.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r20] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | Here ghayr means “not” and lā means “other than,” allowing coordination; when ghayr means “except,” it cannot be coordinated with lā, as in the rejected phrase “I have Abdullah except Zayd.”
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r21] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar read “the path of those whom You favored,” and Baghawi links this to verses describing the Jews as recipients of anger and a people who strayed. | mentions 5:60, 5:77
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r22] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | An unnamed view identifies those angered as the Jews and those astray as the Christians, citing verses on their anger and earlier deviation. | mentions 5:60, 5:77
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r23] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah says those angered are people of innovation.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r24] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah says those astray are people who have left the Sunna.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r25] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | The reader should say Amin after finishing al-Fatiha, separated from it by a brief pause; it may be pronounced short or long.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r26] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | Amin means “O God, hear and answer.”
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r27] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · ابن عباس وقتادة | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada explain Amin as “so it is” or “so be it.”
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r28] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says Amin is one of God's names.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r29] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | Another view calls Amin the seal of supplication.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r3] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | Another view includes everyone God kept firm in faith among the prophets and believers, as in the verse about those favored alongside the prophets. | mentions 4:69
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r30] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | Another view says Amin is God's seal upon His servants, protecting them from afflictions like a letter's seal protects its contents.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r31] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says the final phrase, the congregation should say Amin; imam and angels also say it, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins. Baghawi grades it sahih.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r32] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet tells Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that al-Fatiha has no like in Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an and is the seven oft-repeated given to him; graded hasan sahih. | mentions 8:24
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r33] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas reports that an angel announced two lights never given to a prophet before: al-Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; every letter recited brings a gift. Graded sahih. | mentions 2:285, 2:286
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r34] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is incomplete; Baghawi grades the report sahih.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r35] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · أبو هريرة | reports | When a Persian worshipper asks about praying behind the imam, Abu Hurayra tells him to recite al-Fatiha silently to himself.

[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Those under wrath are people whose path incurred God’s anger; divine anger is the will to punish sinners, but does not befall sinful believers, only disbelievers.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Other explanations call Amin the seal of a supplication or God’s seal protecting servants from harm, like a seal protecting a letter.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r11] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says Amin, worshippers should do so too; angels also say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins. Al-Baghawi grades it sound.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The straying ones are those who departed from guidance; the root sense of straying is perishing or disappearing, like water disappearing into milk.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Here ghayr functions as ‘not,’ which permits coordination with lā; if it meant ‘other than,’ such coordination would be ungrammatical.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Umar’s reading says ‘the path of those You favored, not those under wrath, and not the straying ones.’
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | A reported identification makes the objects of wrath Jews and the straying ones Christians, supported by Quranic descriptions of each group. | mentions 5:60, 5:77
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | Sahl b. Abd Allah interprets those under wrath as innovators and the straying ones as people departing from the Sunnah.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p55/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس وقتادة | reports | Ibn Abbas and Qatada gloss Amin as ‘so be it.’

[KASHSHAF:1:7/r15] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The first ʿalayhim is accusative as object of anʿamta; the second is nominative as agent in the passive phrase.

[KASHSHAF:1:7/r18] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · أيوب السختياني | reports | Ayyub reads with hamza; Amr ibn Ubayd also uses a hamza form.

[KASHSHAF:1:7/r2] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The apposition reinforces and explains the straight path as the Muslims' path, certifying its uprightness emphatically.
[KASHSHAF:1:7/r20] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Amin is a sound-form used as the name of the verb respond, like words meaning wait, hurry, and come.

[KASHSHAF:1:7/r22] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Amin has long and short alif, both attested by poetry.
[KASHSHAF:1:7/r23] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · النبي وجبريل | reports | Gabriel taught the Prophet Amin at the end of al-Fatiha and called it a seal on a book.
[KASHSHAF:1:7/r24] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Amin is not Quran because it was not entered in the codices.

[KASHSHAF:1:7/r9] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Alternatively, ghayr is an adjective: the blessed combine faith with safety from anger and error.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p58#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The phrase is an explanatory substitute for the straight path and virtually repeats the verb, emphasizing and identifying the straight way with the Muslims' way. | mentions 7:75

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p58#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud reads the phrase as the path of those whom You blessed, using a relative pronoun instead of alladhina.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p58#3/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Ghayr al-maghḍūb may substitute for those blessed, describing them as safe from anger and error, or qualify them as combining faith with safety from both.

[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The phrase “the path of those” is a substitute for the previously mentioned straight path.

[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r11] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses’ people before they changed their way; the author says this is the same as the preceding Israelite interpretation.

[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r13] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو العالية | reports | As Makki transmits it, Abū al-ʿĀliya identifies the favored people as Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r14] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | prefers | The author says Abū al-ʿĀliya’s identification makes the straight path the way of Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar; this is stronger because calling the persons themselves a path is figurative.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r15] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads the pronoun with ḍamma on hāʾ and a quiescent mīm; the other readers use kasra on hāʾ and differ over mīm.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r16] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الباقون | reports | The remaining readers pronounce hāʾ with kasra, while differing over the mīm.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r17] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · نافع | reports | Reports give Nāfiʿ a choice between mīm with ḍamma and sukūn; since he did not object to ḍamma, the author infers his own reading used sukūn.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r18] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · عبد الله بن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr links the mīm with a wāw when it is pronounced with ḍamma, whether the preceding hāʾ has ḍamma or kasra.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r19] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ورش | reports | Warsh uses kasra on hāʾ and pauses on mīm, but supplies a pronounced wāw when an original alif follows the mīm. | mentions 2:6
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r2] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · عمر بن الخطاب وابن الزبير | reports | ʿUmar and Ibn al-Zubayr read “the path of those whom You favored” as “the path of whom You favored.”
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r20] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر والكسائي | reports | Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī use kasra on hāʾ and sukūn on mīm in the basic form.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r21] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · عاصم وابن كثير ونافع | reports | Before a following consonant, ʿĀṣim, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ retain kasra on hāʾ but put ḍamma on mīm. | mentions 2:61, 3:112
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r22] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو عمرو | reports | Before a following consonant, Abū ʿAmr uses kasra on both hāʾ and mīm. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 36:14
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r23] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الكسائي | reports | Before a following consonant, al-Kisāʾī uses ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 28:23
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r24] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى | reports | He says hāʾ varies between kasra and ḍamma only when preceded by kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; otherwise hāʾ is ḍamma.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r25] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى | reports | When no hāʾ preceded by kasra or quiescent yāʾ comes before mīm, he allows only mīm with ḍamma or sukūn, as in منكم and أنتم.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r26] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · صاحب الدلائل | reports | He catalogs forms with a wāw after mīm, without the wāw, with mīm ḍamma, and with kasra and yāʾ, reflecting several combinations of vowels.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r27] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinnī transmits from Aḥmad ibn Mūsā forms with an extended wāw, unextended ḍamma, and mīm sukūn; Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid also read with an extended yāʾ.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r28] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الحسن وعمرو بن فائد والأعرج | reports | Additional transmitted forms include kasra on mīm without yāʾ-lengthening and al-Aʿraj’s kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm without lengthening.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r29] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The combinations amount to ten forms: five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with hāʾ kasra, though only six are transmitted from canonical readers.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r3] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The relative plural derives from لذٍ; its yāʾ drops with nunation and returns when the definite article is prefixed.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r30] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي | reports | The majority of named readers read ghayr with kasra; Ibn Kathīr reads it with fatḥa, though kasra is also reported from him.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r31] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو علي | reports | On the genitive reading, ghayr can be an appositive to الذين or an adjective to an indefinite, since الذين here is not specifically singled out.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r32] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو علي | reports | On the accusative reading, ghayr can be circumstantial, exceptive, or an implied direct object of “I mean.”
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r33] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الخليل | reports | A similar account is transmitted from al-Khalīl for the accusative parsing of ghayr.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r34] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو بكر بن السراج | reports | Ibn al-Sarrāj argues that ghayr plus its definite complement is definite here: an understood, unique opposite makes “other than the recipients of favor” identifiable.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r35] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو بكر بن السراج | reports | Ordinarily ghayr and mithl remain indefinite despite annexation because “other than you” and likenesses have innumerable possible referents; a single known opposite makes ghayr definite.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r36] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | He explains that Ibn al-Sarrāj preserves الذين as definite and permits a definite adjective, while others treat ghayr as indefinite and approximate الذين to a general noun.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r37] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | prefers | The author calls the genitive reading the clear choice, noting it is the reading of the majority and is also reported from Ibn Kathīr.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r38] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد وعدي بن حاتم عن النبي | reports | They identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the same interpretation is reported from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim from the Prophet.
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r39] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The author says scripture repeatedly describes God’s wrath against Jews, citing their incurring wrath and the punishment of Sabbath-breakers. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 5:60, 2:65
[IBNATIYYA:1:7/r4] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | الذي is an indefinite, deficient relative noun requiring a clause and a resumptive pronoun; its singular is indeclinable, while its dual forms decline.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p79/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف | reports | Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf reportedly say Amin is one of God's names.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p79/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Another report calls Amin the seal stamped on the books of the people of Paradise who receive them in faith.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p79/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Given these reports, anyone praying or reciting al-Fatiha outside prayer should end the supplication with amin, but outside prayer it is not said aloud in the manner of formal recitation.
[TABRISI:1:7#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh explains kasra on hā after yā or kasra as phonetic lightening and likens it to imāla; a following silent wāw changes to yā after kasra.
[TABRISI:1:7#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ alladhīna is either an adjective of al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm or its apposition; apposition implies repeating the syntactic governor, unlike an adjective. | mentions 7:75
[TABRISI:1:7#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Alladhīna is a relative noun, and anʿamta ʿalayhim is its relative clause; together they form a genitive noun annexed to ṣirāṭ.
[TABRISI:1:7#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | In the genitive, ghayr may be an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim or to alladhīna, or an adjective of the relative phrase despite ghayr usually modifying an indefinite noun.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj allows ghayr as an adjective of alladhīna because the relative phrase does not target named individuals, much like a generic man like you.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي بن عيسى الرماني | reports | Al-Rummani allows the adjective because alladhīna with its clause functions like a common noun rather than a proper name.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو بكر السراج | reports | Al-Sarraj says ghayr becomes definite when its definite complement has one known opposite: the favored people are the ones other than those under anger.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو بكر السراج | reports | In the accusative, ghayr may be a circumstantial qualifier, a disconnected exception, or an explanatory specification meaning 'I mean'.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The word maghdūb need not be pluralized because the plural pronoun in ʿalayhim already marks those who incur anger.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · البصريون | reports | The Basran grammarians take lā as an emphatic extra particle of negation, eliminating an ambiguity that could otherwise allow separate readings of the coordinated words.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans interpret lā as meaning ghayr, so the phrase excludes both the angered and the astray.
[TABRISI:1:7#3/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي بن عيسى الرماني | reports | Al-Rummani explains lā in the exception reading as an extra particle, like in the line about a pit of destruction and the Qur'anic phrase 'that you should not prostrate'. | mentions 7:12
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The favored people are those who obey God and the Messenger, as identified in the verse listing prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous. | mentions 4:69
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The root of niʿma carries the sense of intensification or addition, as in grinding medicine thoroughly.
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · جميع المفسرين | reports | Commentators broadly identify those under anger as Jews, supported by verses about divine anger and the Sabbath violators turned into apes. | mentions 5:60, 2:65
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The astray are identified as Christians, supported by the warning against those who went astray and led many astray. | mentions 5:77
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن البصري | reports | Hasan says both Jews and Christians are both astray and under anger, though God marks each group by a distinguishing epithet despite their shared traits.
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Other interpreters take both descriptions as applying to all unbelievers, with the two attributes conveying different benefits.
[TABRISI:1:7#4/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · عبد القاهر الجرجاني | reports | Al-Jurjani instead reads the language generically as a prayer to avoid a state like that of the angered, not a reference to a particular people.
[TABRISI:1:7#5/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · عبد القاهر الجرجاني | reports | Al-Jurjani says a speaker may ask to join those favored or be spared the state of the angered without referring to any known group; Antara's beloved is likewise not compared to a third person.
[TABRISI:1:7#5/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Divine anger is God's will to impose deserved punishment, curse the people, and disavow them; its root denotes severity.
[TABRISI:1:7#5/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Ḍalāl fundamentally means destruction and, in religion, departure from truth; the author cites 'we were lost in the earth' and 'He destroyed their works'. | mentions 47:8
[TABRISI:1:7#5/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The wording avoids saying that those favored are simply other than the angered, out of courtesy and preference for refined expression.
[TABRISI:1:7#5/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Muhammad ibn Muslim reports al-Sadiq's explanation that the seven oft-repeated verses are the Opening of the Book. | mentions 15:87
[TABRISI:1:7#5/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says God bestowed the Opening of the Book from a treasure of Paradise, including the basmala and the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned. | mentions 17:46
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-ḥamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin is described as the utterance of Paradise's people when they thank God for their good reward.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Universal grace and provision lead to the name Rahman; despite people's shortcomings, God forgives, delays punishment, and does not withdraw His blessings, so He is Rahim.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Because people oppress one another, the worshiper acknowledges a future day when the wronged receive justice from the wrongdoer and says Malik yawm al-din.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Knowing God as Creator, provider, and merciful giver establishes that He alone is worthy of worship; the speaker shifts to direct address as if seeing a king face-to-face.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Conflicting desires, doubts, and opinions leave no helper but God, so the worshiper requests assistance for obedience with all its causes.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · جبرائيل | reports | Gabriel says that whenever a Muslim says 'Lord of the Worlds', God and the inhabitants of heaven affirm him.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Iyyaka naʿbudu expresses pure worship, iyyaka nastaʿīn is the best way to seek needs, and the straight path is the path of the prophets.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | This explanation identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Al-Halabi reports that al-Sadiq read Malik yawm al-din and ihdina ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm; another narration interprets the latter as referring to Ali, the Commander of the Faithful.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Jamil reports al-Sadiq's instruction that a follower behind an imam should say al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin when the imam finishes al-Fatiha.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبد الله | reports | Fudayl ibn Yasar reports al-Sadiq's instruction to say al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin after finishing al-Fatiha.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The sura's sequence begins with recognition of God's visible favors, so the worshiper starts with the basmala as invocation and acknowledgment of the benefactor's divinity and mercy.
[TABRISI:1:7#6/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Recognition of God's favors to oneself and others leads to praise and recognition that He is Lord of all creatures.
[TABRISI:1:7#7/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Having reached knowledge of truth, the worshiper asks for lasting guidance and protection from error because he lacks infallibility; the request includes knowledge of rulings, Islamic practice, and following the divinely appointed Imams.
[TABRISI:1:7#7/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The worshiper asks to join God's chosen beneficiaries and be protected from those who oppose truth, blind themselves to guidance, or doubt clear proofs and stray from the right way.
[TABRISI:1:7/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · حمزة ويعقوب | reports | Hamza pronounces the hā in ʿalayhim and its parallels with ḍamma and the mīm quiescent; Yaqub uses ḍamma on hā preceded by a silent yā in duals and masculine and feminine plurals.
[TABRISI:1:7/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Other transmitted forms vary the hā and mīm, add or omit a linking wāw, or connect it only before a following consonant; the regions and readers differ in these choices.

[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p597/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The first Qur'anic sense is gracious favor, illustrated by the command to remember God's favor and its parallel in al-Ahzab. | mentions 5:11, 33:9
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p597/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A second sense is religion and Scripture, as in warnings against exchanging God's favor after it came. | mentions 2:211, 14:28
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p597/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A third sense is Muhammad, whom people recognize as God's favor and then deny. | mentions 16:83

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p15/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مجاهد وهلال بن يساف وجعفر بن محمد | reports | A third view treats āmīn as one of God's names, held by Mujāhid, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad.

[RAZI:1:7/r17] RAZI, d. 606 · النحويون | reports | Most grammarians define kalima as a single word and kalām as a meaningful sentence; Ibn Jinnī sides with them, though Razi finds his evidence weak.
[RAZI:1:7/r18] RAZI, d. 606 · الأصوليون | reports | Most legal theorists see no difference between kalima and kalām: either term may cover a single utterance or a compound expression.
[RAZI:1:7/r19] RAZI, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi judges Ibn Jinnī's case for distinguishing kalima from kalām weak, resting chiefly on an implication he draws from a statement by Sībawayh.
[RAZI:1:7/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The sūra contains inexhaustible discussions and secrets; the claim that it contains ten thousand questions suits the audience's understanding of its vast implications.
[RAZI:1:7/r20] RAZI, d. 606 · الأصوليون | reports | Legal theorists argue that a single word counts as speech because it opposes silence, affects a listener through meaning, and can naturally be described as something a person said.
[RAZI:1:7/r21] RAZI, d. 606 · زفر | reports | In an unconsummated marriage, Zufar says that repeating the conditional phrase إن كلمتك completes the condition before the divorce clause, so the ensuing divorce does not take effect.
[RAZI:1:7/r22] RAZI, d. 606 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions treat the condition as incomplete until the whole sentence is finished, so one divorce takes effect when the sentence is complete.
[RAZI:1:7/r23] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says the disagreement applies to إن كلمتك فأنت طالق; with إن تكلمت بكلمة, إن نطقت, إن تلفظت بلفظة, or إن قلت قولا, Zufar's view should prevail unanimously.
[RAZI:1:7/r24] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | Scholars disagree whether kalima and kalām include meaningless speech: some say yes because it can be called unused or unintelligible speech, while others require meaningful expression.
[RAZI:1:7/r25] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | Scholars also dispute whether naturally meaningful sounds, such as pain cries, coughs, or bird calls, count as words; the issue affects whether hearing one triggers an oath.
[RAZI:1:7/r26] RAZI, d. 606 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinnī says qawl literally applies to a sentence or a single word, kalām only to a complete sentence, and kalima only to an isolated word; a poem treating qāf as a qawl supports the first distinction.
[RAZI:1:7/r27] RAZI, d. 606 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinnī says qawl can metaphorically mean a belief or opinion, as in attributing a doctrine to Abū Ḥanīfa or Mālik, because belief is apprehended through its expression.
[RAZI:1:7/r28] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Qāla can be used for nonverbal events, as when birds, eyes, or a full basin are said to speak; Razi also cites two Qurʾānic examples of such speech. | mentions 16:40, 41:11
[RAZI:1:7/r29] RAZI, d. 606 · مثبتو كلام النفس | reports | Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech. | mentions 63:1
[RAZI:1:7/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi illustrates how analyzing Aʿūdhu billāh requires definitions and subdivisions of nouns, verbs, particles, and the possible derivations of the name Allah.
[RAZI:1:7/r30] RAZI, d. 606 · عمر | reports | A report from ʿUmar says that at the Saqīfa he had composed words within himself, but Abū Bakr spoke first; Razi gives no grading.

[RAZI:1:7/r32] RAZI, d. 606 · من أنكر كلام النفس | reports | Those denying inner speech argue that someone who neither speaks nor pronounces letters is described as not having spoken, and that oaths attach to uttered words.
[RAZI:1:7/r33] RAZI, d. 606 · بعض أصحابنا | reports | Some of Razi's school hold that qawl and kalām are equivocal terms for both the inward meaning and the spoken expression.
[RAZI:1:7/r34] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Utterances are called aḥādīth because their successive letters occur one after another, or because hearing them brings knowledge and meanings into hearts. | mentions 52:34
[RAZI:1:7/r35] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi lists kalima, kalām, qawl, lafẓ, ʿibāra, ḥadīth, and nuṭq as terms needing comparison, leaving the derivation and precise relation of nuṭq for inquiry.
[RAZI:1:7/r36] RAZI, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi rejects al-Zamakhsharī's definition of kalima as an utterance denoting one simple meaning by convention: past-tense forms and imperative particles convey more than one element.
[RAZI:1:7/r37] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Used expressions divide into a simple form, a compound whose parts signify only in another analysis, and a composed expression whose parts signify independently in every analysis.
[RAZI:1:7/r38] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Meaningful sound has four form-meaning combinations: both simple, both compound, simple form with compound meaning, or compound form with compound meaning; compound form with simple meaning is impossible.
[RAZI:1:7/r39] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi defines kalima as a single conventional utterance signifying a meaning; the definition excludes non-words and compounds through its four restrictions.
[RAZI:1:7/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge.
[RAZI:1:7/r40] RAZI, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi rejects Avicenna's definition of kalima as a single meaningful sound: sound is a remote genus, whereas lafẓ is the more suitable proximate genus.
[RAZI:1:7/r41] RAZI, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazila require an informative word to contain at least two letters; they explain one-letter particles as shortened forms, but Razi notes that many useful particles remain counterexamples.
[RAZI:1:7/r42] RAZI, d. 606 · author | prefers | Razi's preferred definition is anything spoken that conveys something by convention; it includes simple and compound forms while excluding writing and gesture.
[RAZI:1:7/r43] RAZI, d. 606 · عباد | reports | ʿAbbād holds that words naturally signify their meanings; Razi rejects this because natural properties do not vary across places and times, and answers that conventional assignments need not be unmotivated.
[RAZI:1:7/r44] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Some words imitate their referents' sounds: qaṭā and laqlaq echo birds, while khaḍm and qaḍm distinguish eating moist and dry foods; Ibn Jinnī gives further examples.
[RAZI:1:7/r45] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says one cannot decide whether language was divinely instituted: the regress argument for divine origin and the appeal to God's teaching Adam both admit alternatives. | mentions 2:31
[RAZI:1:7/r46] RAZI, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazila argue that conventional language must be created by humans, since necessary knowledge that God assigned words would entail necessary knowledge of God and undermine moral responsibility.
[RAZI:1:7/r47] RAZI, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi answers that God could create necessary knowledge that a human assigner fixed a word's meaning without revealing that the assigner was God.
[RAZI:1:7/r48] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the proofs are inconclusive, Razi allows that all languages are divinely instituted, all conventional, or partly each.
[RAZI:1:7/r49] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | A simple word cannot explain its own meaning from scratch without circularity, since recognizing its convention requires prior awareness of the word and meaning; learned association resolves the problem.
[RAZI:1:7/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | At the furthest epistemological stage, he asks how the unknown can be judged contrary to the known if its nature is unknown, since that judgment would make it known.
[RAZI:1:7/r50] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The circularity problem does not apply to compounds: convention supplies the simple meanings, and reason combines them to understand the compound.
[RAZI:1:7/r51] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Words signify mental conceptions rather than external objects: changing one's perception of a distant object changes the name used, and contradictory propositions do not make the world both old and originated.
[RAZI:1:7/r52] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Not every essence can receive a name, because essences are unlimited and an unapprehended item cannot be individually conceived for naming.
[RAZI:1:7/r53] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Concepts most necessary to communicate, such as commands, prohibitions, generality, and specification, are likeliest to receive words because need supplies strong motivation.
[RAZI:1:7/r54] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | A familiar word cannot name a hidden concept unknown to the public: motion names observable transition, not a subtle cause; likewise knowledge and power name the evident state, not its hidden ground.
[RAZI:1:7/r55] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Maʿnā denotes the mental conception intended by a speaker; an external thing is called a meaning only derivatively, as what the conception concerns.
[RAZI:1:7/r56] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Some distinctions cannot be defined verbally because language lacks a dedicated term, as with kinds of sweetness; private experiences are also indefinable to listeners who have never conceived them.
[RAZI:1:7/r57] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Language serves humans' need to communicate what is in their minds to obtain help; compared with writing, gestures, or clapping, speech is easy to produce, temporary, and combinatorially abundant.

olds | Human perfection is knowledge of truth and action upon good; the body, heart, and respiratory system serve that end, with breathing cooling the heart and expelled air becoming the material of sound.

[RAZI:1:7/r62] RAZI, d. 606 · أصحابنا | prefers | Razi's school distinguishes inward request from will and mental judgment from belief; God's command that an unbeliever believe is not evidence that He wills that belief.

[RAZI:1:7/r7] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi distinguishes ordinary derivation from greater derivation, which studies permutations of a word's consonants; he gives 2, 6, 24, and 120 permutations for words of two through five letters.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break. | mentions 9:119
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen. | mentions 53:9
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The spiritual ascent rises through human spirits, the spirits of the heavens, angels, throne-bearers, and pure spirits detached from bodies, whose worship and love of God exceed human comprehension. | mentions 39:75, 69:17, 21:20, 12:76

[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The worshipper should view worship from God's perspective and so regard it as inadequate, never suppose that personal worship gives one a claim on God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The soul is softened by awe like wood before fire; bend it in bowing, then let it straighten and practice religion gently.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The bow and two prostrations overcome three ruinous obstacles: desire, anger, and caprice.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In the closing sitting, greetings are offered by the tongue, prayers by the limbs, and good words by the heart and faith.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The prayer opens a gate of knowledge, followed by remembrance in the basmala and gratitude in the praise of God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The names al-Rahman and al-Rahim signify the gates of hope, while Master of Judgment signifies fear.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p222/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The final clause is the gate of following and being guided by pure spirits.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p223/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A divine report says God remembers a servant in a gathering better than the servant's; the angels then long to visit, and the worshipper greets them on both sides.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p223/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Space and time are the most imposing created realities: space is boundless expanse, while time is an imagined span from eternity past to eternity future.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p227/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A report attributed to Ali says God created intellect from a hidden light, endowed it with virtues, and had it first speak praise; God said no creature was dearer to Him.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p228/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Some reports add al-Hamd, al-Hamid, and al-Mahmud among the Prophet's names, making five names associated with mercy; paired with five divine mercy terms, they give the sinner ten oceans of mercy. | mentions 15:49, 21:107, 7:156

[RAZI-FULL:v1p229/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Five kinds of qibla—Jerusalem, the Kaaba, the Frequented House, the Throne, and God's presence—are assigned to the five names.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p229/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The first half of Fatiha sends the lights of five divine names down and the second half sends the servant's five petitions upward, with the transition at Master of Judgment and You alone we worship.

[QASHANI:1:6-7/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Those under wrath are like Jews who stop at outward forms and bodily pleasures, veiling themselves from spiritual truths and intellectual delight; wrath entails expulsion, distance, and darkness of appearances.
[QASHANI:1:6-7/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The astray are like Christians who stop at inner lights and special mercy, overlooking God’s outward manifestation and losing vision of the beloved’s beauty throughout creation.
[QASHANI:1:6-7/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Muhammadan unifiers answer the calls to seek pardon and paradise, fear God and believe His messenger, and worship God without partners, thereby combining love of the essence’s beauty with the attributes’ goodness. | mentions 3:133, 57:28, 4:36
[QASHANI:1:6-7/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The unified path joins hope and fear, prayer for complete light, steadfastness, gardens, reward and light, seeing God’s face wherever one turns, and the best reward with increase. | mentions 17:57, 66:8, 41:30, 98:8, 57:19, 2:115, 10:26
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r1] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The relative pronoun الذين is most eloquently declined with yāʾ in all three cases, though some Arabs use wāw in the nominative; dropping its nūn is permitted, though some restrict that to poetic necessity.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r10] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawī says a report from the Prophet explains the path as God's Book or faith and its concomitants, Islam and its laws, or the moderate way.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r11] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو العالية والحسن | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya and al-Hasan identify the path as the way of the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r12] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · فضيل بن عياض | reports | Fudayl b. ʿIyāḍ interprets the straight path as the way of pilgrimage.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r13] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عثمان | reports | ʿUthmān interprets the straight path as the Sunan.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r14] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd b. Jubayr interpre
<<part 24 ends; continues in part 25>>

<<1:7 notes, part 25 of 0..49>>
ts the straight path as the way to Paradise.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r15] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · القشيري | reports | Al-Qushayrī interprets the straight path as the way of Sunna and the community.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r16] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الترمذي | reports | Al-Tirmidhī interprets the straight path as the way of fear and hope.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r17] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عمرو بن عبيد | reports | ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd interprets the straight path as the bridge over Hell.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r18] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | One Sufi reading asks for guidance through becoming absent from the path, so that one is not bound to the path; Abū Ḥayyān says such readings do not follow the wording, while acknowledging their experiential insight.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r19] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الجنيد | reports | Al-Junayd says asking for guidance amid bewilderment is among the clearest pre-eternal attributes; the request seeks the qualities of servanthood to avoid absorption in those attributes.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r2] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Grammarians disagree about how الذين is recognized; unlike الذي, it is restricted to rational beings.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r20] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الفخر الرازي | reports | Al-Rāzī rejects identifying the path as the Qurʾān or Islam and its laws because those favored people supposedly lived before the Qurʾān and this Islamic dispensation.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r21] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān says al-Rāzī's objection works only if the favored people are proved to be pre-Islamic; the source will report differing identifications of them, so that premise is unsettled.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r22] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The request for guidance follows naturally from the preceding declaration of worship and reliance: worship is sound only through guidance to the clear route that reaches its goal.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r23] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الحسن والضحاك | reports | Al-Hasan and al-Dahhāk read صراطاً مستقيماً without the definite article; صراط الذين then apposes a definite expression to an indefinite one, as in 42:52. | mentions 42:52
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r24] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq reads صراط مستقيم with an annexation, meaning the upright religion; with this and the majority reading, صراط الذين is a clarifying apposition of one definite expression to another.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r25] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The apposition identifies the somewhat ambiguous previously mentioned straight path, repeats the request for emphasis, and directs it to the route of those favored.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r26] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | A rare alternative says the second path is different from the first, as if a conjunction had been read between them; the commentators disagree about what this second path denotes.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r27] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad says the path is knowledge of God and understanding Him.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r28] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Other explanations identify the path as observing the obligations and following the Sunan, or as inward agreement with outward practice in the completion of blessing.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r29] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The explanation of inward and outward blessing is linked to 31:20, which says God has poured out both manifest and hidden blessings upon you. | mentions 31:20
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r3] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Niʿma denotes ease and softness of living; the south wind and ostrich are also named from softness, and anʿama ʿalayhi means to bestow abundantly.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r30] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن مسعود وعمر وابن الزبير وزيد بن علي | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Zayd b. ʿAlī read صراط من أنعمت عليهم.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r31] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Among the proposed referents of those favored are prophets, angels, and the unaltered communities of Moses and Jesus; Abū Ḥayyān lists these as alternatives rather than restricting the wording to one group.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r32] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās is cited for identifying those favored as believers.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r33] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن عطية عن ابن عباس والجمهور | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority mean the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, deriving this from 4:69. | mentions 4:69
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r34] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan identifies those favored as the Companions of the Prophet.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r35] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · فرقة | reports | One group identifies those favored as the believers among the Children of Israel.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r36] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses' followers before they changed their religion.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r37] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda limits those favored to the prophets.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r38] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو العالية | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya identifies those favored as Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r39] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · وكيع | reports | Wakīʿ identifies those favored as Muslims.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r4] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Anʿama is one of twenty-four functions of the form أفعل: it makes someone possess the base noun, while implying benefaction and taking على instead of its original direct object.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r40] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording leaves the blessing unrestricted, so it can encompass every kind of blessing through a general use of the category.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r41] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Proposed explanations of God's favor include creating people for felicity, rescuing them from destruction, and guiding them to follow the Messenger; the wording itself does not specify a restriction.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r42] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazila affirm that God bestows blessing on unbelievers, while other theologians deny it.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r43] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The prepositional phrase عليهم is in the accusative position because it is governed by an active verb; the same applies to a preposition governed by a non-passive verb or equivalent.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r44] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The active attribution of favor appeals for acceptance of the request: since God has already favored them, answering their plea for guidance is consistent with His beneficence.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r45] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The prayer asks that guidance to the path of the favored continue: those who praise God and declare worship and reliance already possess guidance, but ask for its permanence.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r46] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Ghayr is always masculine singular; it expresses difference in some respect, originates as an adjective, can mark exception, and remains annexed. It cannot take al and does not ordinarily become definite by annexation.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r47] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Ibn al-Sarrāj says ghayr becomes definite when its complement is one specified entity; Sībawayh allows a non-pure annexation to become definite by intent. The commentators also discuss its fronting in predication.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r48] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | In predication, ghayr or mithl tends to precede its complement; the cited line means the speaker is unlike people who are deceived, and reversed order would distort the point.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r49] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Anger is a change in disposition caused by something disliked; it can also mean turning away, since turning away is one consequence of anger.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r5] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The attached tāʾ is the second-person masculine singular pronoun; أنت consists of two pronouns and is a compound.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r50] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Lā can be a particle of negation, prohibition, or augmentation; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the Kufan view that it can be a noun.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r51] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Ḍalāl can mean ruin, concealment, loss, ignorance of an object's location, waste, neglect, forgetting, departure from the proper route, bewilderment, or hesitation; Qurʾanic usage also includes lack of detailed knowledge and love.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r52] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | The majority read ghayr in the genitive; al-Khalīl reports Ibn Kathīr's accusative reading, also attributed to ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r53] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī parses genitive ghayr as an apposition either to الذين or to the pronoun in عليهم; Abū Ḥayyān calls both analyses weak because apposition by an adjective is weak.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r54] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh parses genitive ghayr as an adjective, treating it as definite through annexation to عليهم; Ibn al-Sarrāj offers a different account of its definiteness.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r55] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | The suggestion that الذين denotes a generic class, allowing ghayr to modify it despite definiteness, undermines the rule that a definite noun is modified only by a definite; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this account.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r56] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawī and others parse accusative ghayr as a circumstantial accusative from عليهم, or from الذين; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the latter because the genitive complement has no syntactic position for a circumstantial modifier.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r57] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الأخفش والزجاج | reports | Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj allow accusative ghayr as a disconnected exception because the preceding wording does not include those who are astray; some readers reject this analysis because of lā.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r58] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Some permit accusative ghayr as an exception by treating lā as extra, since they say lā is extra only after prior negation; they cite Qurʾanic and poetic exampl
