es, while other grammarians take lā as genuinely negative.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r59] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān says the alleged proof that lā is extra in the verse of the generous man is not decisive: lā itself is the object of أبى, and البخل is its apposition or a causal object.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r6] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Most grammarians treat على as a preposition; Sībawayh and a group of later Basran grammarians treat it as a ظرف noun except in certain constructions. It can express literal or figurative elevation and several other relations.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r60] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الخليل | reports | An alternative analysis, attributed to al-Khalīl, treats ghayr as an accusative with an implicit أعني, 'I mean'.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r61] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The phrase عليهم is in the nominative position as the passive verb's deputy subject; grammarians dispute whether a prepositional phrase can occupy that role.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r62] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Lā reinforces the negation already contained in ghayr and is attached to المغضوب عليهم to avoid suggesting that الضالين is coordinated with الذين.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r63] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عمر وأبي | reports | ʿUmar and Ubayy read غير الضالين, with reports of both accusative and genitive on the rāʾ in the two occurrences; Abū Ḥayyān says the reading marks the angered and astray as distinct, while lā is the likelier emphasis.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r64] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī uses the alleged parallel between ghayr and lā to allow a governed object before ghayr; Abū Ḥayyān calls the argument very weak, since similarity of meaning does not transfer syntax without Arabic attestation.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r65] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | Some supply an omitted صراط before ghayr; Abū Ḥayyān finds the estimate weak because it creates awkward apposition or adjective order and other difficult attachment analyses.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r66] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أيوب السختياني | reports | Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads ولا الضألين, turning the alif into hamza to avoid two adjacent sukūns; Abū Ḥayyān says the sound change is not productive, though Abū Zayd and Abū al-Fatḥ attest it as a dialect and cite Arab usage and poetry.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r67] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The relative clause of الذين uses a past verb to make God's favor definite and established; the clause with أل uses a participle encompassing all times, and makes the anger passive rather than directly ascribing it to God.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r68] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r69] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The blessing intended is religious; those angered and those astray are general categories covering everyone who incurs anger or goes astray.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r7] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The suffix هم is a masculine plural pronoun referring to rational absent people, and it can occupy nominative, accusative, or genitive position.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r70] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r71] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عدي بن حاتم عن رسول الله | reports | The Jews-and-Christians identification is also related from ʿAdī b. Ḥātim from the Prophet; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be adopted if the report is sound.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r72] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Another reported identification makes those angered the Jews and those astray the polytheists; Abū Ḥayyān notes other views without specifying them here.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r73] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | A Sufi restriction interprets those angered as people who neglect proper courtesy while serving God, and the astray as those who perceive that conduct; Abū Ḥayyān says the wording does not support such restrictions.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r74] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | God's anger may mean His intent to requite a sinner, making it an attribute of essence because His knowledge precedes creation and sin; alternatively it is imposing punishment, an attribute of action.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r75] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Anger precedes misguidance in the wording although it results from it because it contrasts with favor: favor brings good and requital brings harm; the order also suits the sūra's cadence.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r76] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The conjunctive wāw does not itself establish temporal priority; if Jews and Christians are intended, the order may reflect chronology or the Jews' greater hostility, as they came earlier.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r77] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The sūra's closing phrases are an instance of parallel cadence (sajʿ mutawāzī), with the final words matching in meter and rhyme; the author also lists specification, apposition, and word order among its rhetorical features.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r78] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Abū Ḥayyān concludes that the sūra is seven verses by consensus apart from disregarded dissent; Meccan and Kufan counters differ over whether the basmala or صراط الذين is an āya, while ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd counts eight and Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī six.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r79] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | He says the basmala at each sūra's opening is not an āya, while Ibn al-Mubārak anomalously counted it as an āya in every sūra; Abū Ḥayyān says he does not know the principle behind determining āya length.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r8] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | The ten reported pronunciations vary the hāʾ and mīm between ḍamma and kasra, mīm sukūn or vowel, and a following yāʾ or wāw: Hamza, the majority, al-Hasan, Ibn Kathīr, Qālūn, al-Aʿraj, and al-Khaffāf are among those named; Ibn Mujāhid adds ʿUmar b. Fāʾid, and ʿAmr b. Fāʾid is also cited.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r80] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Reports about the sūra's letter count, supposed occasions of revelation, basmala's merit, and many titles are not necessarily causes of revelation or core tafsīr; only sound Prophetic clarification, occasions, and abrogation are indispensable to tafsīr.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r81] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The word Āmīn is not Qurʾān; Abū Ḥayyān omits discussion of its forms, meaning, and prayer ruling, along with introductory istiʿādha, as material outside his intended tafsīr scope.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:7/r9] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · علي | reports | Ali identifies the straight path as the Qurʾān; Ibn ʿAbbās is also cited for this interpretation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p45/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Alladhīna is a relative pronoun, usually yāʾ in every case but sometimes wāw in the nominative; it refers to rational beings, unlike alladhī.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p45/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Deleting the nūn of the relative pronoun is allowed, though some grammarians restrict it to poetic necessity unless it is not for specification.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p45/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Niʿma is ease and comfort; anʿamta makes someone possess a blessing, with ʿalā arising through an added sense of gracious favor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p45/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Anʿama illustrates one of the twenty-four meanings of form IV, making its object a possessor of the root's meaning, here a blessing.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأكثرون | reports | Most grammarians treat ʿalā as a preposition, but Sībawayh treats it as a locative noun except in set uses; its main sense is literal or figurative elevation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | ʿAlā can also mean about, with, in, alongside, because of, from, or serve as an extra particle.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The pronoun hum is masculine plural and rational, and is inflected for nominative, accusative, and genitive positions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · حمزة | reports | Among ten reported forms of ʿalayhim, Ḥamza reads the hāʾ with ḍamma and the mīm quiescent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read the hāʾ of ʿalayhim with kasra and leave the mīm quiescent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan lengthens the kasra of hāʾ and mīm with a following yāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن كثير وقالون | reports | Ibn Kathīr and, in one report, Qālūn use kasra on hāʾ, ḍamma on mīm, and a following wāw.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p46/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأعرج والخفاف عن أبي عمرو | reports | Abū Ḥayyān lists forms that lengthen the mīm with wāw or omit it, and other combinations of hāʾ and mīm vowels, among the ten reported ʿalayhim readings.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq reads “straight path” in annexation, meaning the religion that is upright.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to identify those favored as believers.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · وكيع | reports | Wakīʿ identifies those favored as prophets and believers, or as Muslims.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the majority’s identification to the four groups named in 4:69, and also records Ibn ʿAbbās’s view that they are believers. | mentions 4:69
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan identifies the favored people as the Companions of Muḥammad.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · فرقة | reports | One group identifies them as the believing Israelites.

:v1p48/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses’s followers before they altered the message.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On al-Ḥasan’s and al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s reading, “the path of those” is a definite apposition to an indefinite, like “a straight path, God’s path.” | mentions 43:52
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On al-Ṣādiq’s and the majority’s readings, “the path of those” is an apposition of one definite to another, clarifying the previously somewhat vague “straight path.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | This apposition restates the request for guidance, making it firmer and more emphatic by directing it to the path of those God favored.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A rare interpretation says the second path is not the first, as though a conjunction had been read; interpreters differ over its identification.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad identifies the favored path as knowledge of God and understanding from Him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation identifies the path as fulfilling religious obligations and following the Prophetic sunna.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation makes the path harmony between inward and outward states in the fullness of divine favor. | mentions 31:20
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read “the path of those whom You favored” without the relative pronoun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو العالية | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya identifies those favored as Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Ghayr” is masculine singular by default; feminine agreement may follow its form or its meaning, and it denotes some kind of difference.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Ghayr” is originally an adjective, can mark exception, must be annexed, and cannot take the definite article or become definite merely through annexation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن السراج | reports | Ibn al-Sarrāj holds that “ghayr” becomes definite by annexation when the thing it differs from is a single definite referent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh allows a normally non-defining annexation to become defining when it is intended as such, making “ghayr” definite with a definite complement.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · البيانيون | reports | Rhetoricians say “ghayr” or “mithl” is nearly required before the predicate in examples where it means anyone sharing the stated quality.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The rhetoricians mean that anyone sharing the described quality is expected by analogy and custom to act in the stated way.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording leaves divine favor unrestricted, so it encompasses every kind of favor; the text supplies no basis for narrowing it to a particular favor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Some say God favored them by creating them for felicity; others say He rescued them from ruin, or guided them to follow the Messenger.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Sufi writers add many restrictions, but the wording does not support assigning the favor one particular restriction.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazilites affirm that God bestows favor on unbelievers, while others deny it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Upon them” is syntactically accusative, as are prepositional phrases attached to an active verb or equivalent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The active “You favored” gently appeals to God’s prior generosity to secure acceptance of the plea for continued guidance, like reminding a benefactor of his customary kindness.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p49/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The usual Arabic construction changes the verb’s person with an attached pronoun, though another dialect keeps it unchanged.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Al-maghdūb ʿalayhim” means those incurred anger; anger can also mean turning away because that is one of its consequences.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The particle lā serves negation, command, or redundancy; contrary to the Kufans, it is not a noun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The non-majority genitive reading of “ghayr”; al-Khalīl reports Ibn Kathīr’s accusative reading, also attributed to ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī, and Ibn al-Zubayr.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī analyzes the genitive as an apposition to “those” or to the pronoun in “upon them,” but Abū Ḥayyān says both are weak because “ghayr” is adjectival.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh permits the genitive as an adjective, taking “ghayr” as definite through annexation; Abū Ḥayyān also reports Ibn al-Sarrāj’s narrower rationale and rejects a generic-plural rationale.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawī and others take the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from “those”; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it because the annexed complement has no syntactic position.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p50/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The poetic line means its speaker is unlike people easily deceived; reversing the placement of “ghayr” reverses the intended meaning.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash, al-Zajjāj, and others treat the accusative as a disconnected exception; al-Qurrāʾ object because of the following lā.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القراء | reports | Al-Qurrāʾ allow lā to be extra only after a prior negation, citing poetic usage and 17:61; Abū Ḥayyān discusses competing analyses of the cited poems. | mentions 17:61
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Against interpreters who call lā redundant in the verse about “my generosity,” he argues it is the object of “refused”; “al-bukhl” is an apposition or purpose object.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الخليل | reports | A further analysis attributed to al-Khalīl supplies an implied “I mean” before “ghayr.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Upon them” is nominative as the passive subject of “incurred anger”; grammarians discuss when a prepositional phrase may stand as passive subject.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The lā before “those astray” reinforces negation; placing it in the coordination prevents “those astray” from being mistaken as part of “those You favored.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمر | reports | ʿUmar and Ubayy read “and not those astray” with “ghayr”; variants are also reported for the case ending of rāʾ, distinguishing the two groups.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p51/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī introduces a grammatical example to illustrate the semantic closeness of ghayr and lā.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Putting favor in the verbal relative clause of “those” fixes it to an established act, while the participial “incurred anger” leaves its time broad; the past verb specifies confirmed favor.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The cited poetry illustrates the hamza substitution; if it is a dialect as Abū al-Fatḥ says, Abū Ḥayyān reasons that the substitution should be productive.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The passive “incurred anger” avoids directly attributing anger to God in a humble plea for kindness, and prepares the parallel ending “those astray.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The intended favor is religious; “those angered” and “those astray” are general categories of everyone who incurs anger and goes astray.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عدي بن حاتم | reports | This Jews-and-Christians interpretation is also reported from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim from the Prophet; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be followed if authentic.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Other identifications say the angered are Jews and polytheists; Sufi restrictions also circulate but are not supported by the verse’s wording.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Divine anger can mean the will to punish, an attribute of essence given God’s prior knowledge, or the act of inflicting punishment, an attribute of action.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Anger precedes misguidance despite resulting from

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | If the groups mean Jews and Christians, Jews come first because they appeared earlier or are more hostile.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī argues that “ghayr” allows an object before it, just as lā does, and uses this to establish their grammatical and semantic similarity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān calls al-Zamakhsharī’s argument very weak: the construction is disputed, similarity in meaning does not transfer syntax, and “أنا زيدا غير ضارب” is unattested.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Supplying an omitted “path” before “ghayr” yields weak analyses, including an adjective before its apposition or repeated apposition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أيوب السختياني | reports | Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads “wa-laḍ-ḍāllīn” with a hamza in place of the long vowel to avoid two adjacent vowelless letters.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The hamza substitution occurs in words such as dāba and shāba, but it is too rare to be treated as a productive rule, despite Abū al-Fatḥ’s dialect argument.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p52/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd records dāba and shāba as dialect examples; he first thought ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd had misread until he heard the forms from Arabs.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some analyses posit omitted “path” before “not angered,” while other syntactic choices create many further ellipses in the sūra.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The sūra uses fronting and delay in “we worship, we seek help” and in “those angered, those astray.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The apposition “the path of those whom You favored” is explicit clarification after the initially vague “straight path.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون | reports | The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Alladhīna is genitive through annexation, a relative plural requiring a clause and resumptive; it usually has yāʾ in all cases, though some raise it with wāw, as in the cited verse.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A poetic form uses alladhūna with nominative wāw, and another deletes the relative's nūn to lengthen its clause; the plural is restricted to rational beings unlike singular alladhī.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Anʿamta is the relative clause: tāʾ is its attached nominative second-person subject, and ʿalayhim is governed by the verb and supplies the resumptive pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The causative hamza in anʿamta normally makes the object directly governed, but here the verb is cast with the prepositional government of tafaḍḍala.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The hamza pattern afʿala has many meanings: causation, abundance, becoming, assistance, removal, offering, finding, reaching number, time or place, and lexical relations to other patterns.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Further afʿala meanings include naming, prayer, deserving, conveying, greeting, arriving with something, distinguishing forms, and attacking; the passage illustrates each with examples.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ʿAlā primarily signals literal or figurative elevation; it can also mean ʿan, bi, fī, accompaniment, causation, min, or be augmentative, with Qur'anic and poetic examples. | mentions 7:105, 2:102, 2:177, 2:185, 23:5-6
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ʿAlā can be a noun meaning above when preceded by a preposition, and may be nominal where treating it as a preposition would produce an impermissible link between detached and attached pronouns.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The claim that ʿalā is also a verb because ʿalā Zayd means Zayd rose confuses unrelated words: the verb derives from ʿuluww, unlike the noun or preposition.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The pronoun hāʾ is normally damma, but non-Hijazis use kasra after a silent yāʾ or kasra; mīm is usually silent before a vowel and kasra before silence when hāʾ is kasra.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو بكر ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbārī records ten pronunciations of ʿalayhim, including variations in hāʾ and mīm vowels and added wāw or yāʾ; some were read in Qur'anic recitation.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ghayr is an indefinite apposition to alladhīna; calling it an adjective is difficult because ghayr is indefinite and the relative is definite.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · some grammarians | reports | Two defenses of adjectival ghayr are offered: it becomes definite between opposites, per Ibn al-Sarrāj's weak view, or the relative resembles an indefinite through ambiguity.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مكي | reports | Makkī says ghayr replaces the attached pronoun in ʿalayhim; the author objects that deleting the replaced pronoun would leave the relative clause without its resumptive.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-maghḍūb is genitive by annexation and a passive participle; the prepositional phrase supplies its agent, and the relative al means those who were angered.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ghayr remains masculine singular, though its verb may be feminine when it refers to a woman; it is inherently adjectival and does not become definite through annexation.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ghayr can function like illā for exception, as an adjective by analogy with illā, or like lā for negation, permitting its governed object to precede it.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The poetic line places the object before negative ghayr, meaning the speaker is not unremembered by the beloved despite distance.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Object-fronting is not permitted when ghayr is non-negative; grammarians also differ between a general ban and a distinction for oath responses.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ghayr must be annexed overtly or implicitly, so putting the definite article on it is incorrect.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Ghayr is also read in the accusative as a circumstantial from alladhīna or ʿalayhim, or as a disjoint exception; al-Farrāʾ rejects the latter because lā lacks a preceding negation.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ argues lā is only augmentative after an earlier negation; the cited lines are offered in reply as cases without one.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Calling lā augmentative does not by itself answer al-Farrāʾ; the reply should show examples where it is augmentative without prior negation, while another analysis makes lā the object of abā.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl is reported to parse accusative ghayr with an omitted aʿnī, meaning I mean those other than the angered ones.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | An omitted ṣirāṭ after ghayr is proposed, but this adjective analysis is weak because when an adjective and apposition coexist, the adjective ordinarily comes first; ghayr can instead modify ṣirāṭ alladhīna.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Accusative ghayr may also replace either ṣirāṭ, despite a possible repeated-apposition problem, or serve as a circumstantial from either one.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | If ghayr is adjectival, the analysis must either treat ghayr as definite or treat its relative antecedent as indefinite-like through ambiguity.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Lā reinforces the negation already carried by ghayr and blocks reading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those blessed; Kufans instead equate it with ghayr, and ʿUmar reportedly read that way.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A rare hamzated reading of al-ḍāllīn is supported by dialectal examples; al-Zamakhsharī says it avoids two quiescent consonants, but examples without that environment suggest a regular dialect.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The past-tense relative clause presents God's blessing as established, while the noun after al generalizes across times; passive wording tactfully avoids attributing anger directly to the deity.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Inʿām is delivering benefit to another and is said only of rational recipients, not horses or donkeys.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Anger is described as the heart's blood surging in intent to take revenge; a prophetic report warns against anger and describes its bodily signs.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | When attributed to God, anger means retribution; غضبت لفلان is said of a living person and غضبت به of a dead one.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternative definitions make anger a heart's change toward something disliked, or distinguish divine action-attribute when it means punishment from essent

[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ḍalāl may mean concealment or disappearance, destruction, deviation from the straight path, or forgetfulness; the forgetfulness sense in 2:282 is supported by its following remembrance clause. | mentions 32:10, 2:282
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Amin is not part of the Quran by consensus; it means respond and is an indeclinable imperative noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | rejects | Abu al-Baqa rejects treating Amin as a divine name because a singular definite vocative should take damma and divine names require transmitted authorization.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفارسي | reports | Al-Farisi explains the divine-name reading by an implicit pronoun referring to God within the imperative noun; the author calls this a good analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#7/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Amin has long and short forms, each attested in poetry.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#8/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some treat the long form as foreign because its pattern resembles Qābīl and Hābīl; geminating mīm is commonly called erroneous, though transmitted from al-Ḥasan and Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#8/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الجوهري | reports | Al-Jawhari transmits the common judgment that geminating mim is erroneous, though the reading is also reported from al-Hasan and Jafar al-Sadiq.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7#8/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Faḍl derives the geminated form from amma, to intend or aim toward God, as in the Qur'anic phrase about those intending the Sacred House. | mentions 5:2
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ alladhīna is a complete apposition, a definite noun replacing another definite noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Grammarians enumerate seven kinds of apposition; the first three are undisputed, while some assert apposition of clarification and cite a prayer report, which does not apply to Qur'anic wording.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ذي الرمة | reports | Dhū al-Rumma's line is cited for apposition by mistake or forgetfulness because ḥawa is pure black and laʿas is black tinged with red; the author says these do not occur in eloquent speech.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Arguments for whole-from-part apposition in the Ṭalḥa and Imruʾ al-Qays lines fail: the first reflects an omitted annexed noun, and the second treats a day as a time-span.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad says the second ṣirāṭ differs from the first and denotes knowledge of God; the author finds the required omitted conjunction problematic.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Apposition may be definite or indefinite, overt or pronominal in several combinations; its function is clarification after ambiguity and semantic emphasis through an implied repetition of the governing word.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الله تعالى | reports | In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r1] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | “Path of those You favored” explains the straight path; grammatically it may be apposition or explanatory apposition.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r10] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari reports an accusative circumstantial reading of ghayr, attributed to the Prophet and ʿUmar and also transmitted from Ibn Kathir; its circumstantial referent is the pronoun in ʿalayhim.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The favored path belongs to people of guidance, uprightness, obedience to God and His messengers, and compliance with commands and prohibitions.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r12] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Those subject to anger know the truth but turn away; the astray lack knowledge and wander without reaching the truth.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r13] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The added negation marks two distinct corrupt routes, those of the Jews and Christians.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r14] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعض النحاة | reports | Some grammarians take ghayr as an exception, making it a disconnected exception because the angered are outside the favored group; Ibn Kathir says his own account is better.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r15] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | prefers | Ibn Kathir prefers construing ghayr as “the path other than that of the angered,” with the omitted noun supplied by context.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r16] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The Nabigha al-Dhubyani line illustrates omitting the described noun and retaining its adjective; here “path” is omitted before “other than the angered.”
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r17] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعض النحاة | reports | Some grammarians call la before the astray redundant and cite an al-ʿAjjaj line; Ibn Kathir rejects this and treats it as reinforcing the negation.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r18] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar read “and other than the astray”; Ibn Kathir says this report has a sound chain and treats it as explanatory, supporting emphatic negation and separation of the two paths.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r19] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبي بن كعب | reports | A similar reading is attributed to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb; Ibn Kathir understands it as explanatory rather than as the verse's wording.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r2] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The favored people are the four groups named in 4:69: prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and the righteous. | mentions 4:69, 4:70
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r20] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Jews are characterized by abandoning known truth and thus anger, while Christians seek a goal without knowledge of its way because they do not follow the true Messenger; each group is also both astray and under anger.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r21] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The Qurʾan calls the Jews recipients of anger and specifically describes Christians as astray, supporting the verse's characteristic labels. | mentions 5:60, 5:77
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r22] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Qurʾanic references to Jewish anger and wrongdoing support the identification: Israel's children incur anger for rejecting revelation and are condemned for sin and failure to stop wrongdoing. | mentions 2:90, 5:60, 5:78, 5:79
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r23] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the report from ʿAdi ibn Hatim, the Prophet identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians; al-Tirmidhi grades this route hasan gharīb, and Ibn Kathir notes other routes and wordings.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r24] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | At Wadi al-Qura the Prophet points to Jews as the angered and Christians as the astray; other transmitters send the report without naming the eyewitness, while ʿUrwa's route names Ibn ʿUmar.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r25] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو ذر | reports | A report from Abu Dharr gives the same Prophetic explanation; Ibn Hajar calls Ibn Mardawayh's chain hasan.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r26] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, and Companions of the Prophet, identifies the Jews as angered and Christians as astray.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r27] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas, through al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj, gives the same identification; al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, and others agree, and Ibn Abi Hatim reports no disagreement among exegetes.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r28] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | A report about Zayd ibn ʿAmr says he refused Jewish or Christian conversion because each demanded a share in divine anger, remained on his natural disposition and avoided idols, while his companions became Christians; Waraqa later accepted the Prophet's revelation.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r29] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Scholars may excuse confusing dād and ẓāʾ because their articulation points are close and both are voiced, fricative, and emphatic; the saying “I am the most eloquent to pronounce dād” has no basis.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r3] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | In al-Dahhak's report, the favored path is obedience and worship, including angels, prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous; Ibn Kathir calls this the broadest account. | mentions 4:69
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r30] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The surah praises and magnifies God through His names and attributes, recalls the afterlife, teaches supplication, disavowal of human power, sincere worship and divine oneness, and asks for guidance and steadfastness on the upright religion.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r31] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The requested straight path leads to crossing the eschatological bridge and reaching Paradise with prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous; the surah urges good deeds and warns against false paths.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r32] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The verse attributes favor directly to God, leaves the agent of anger unexpressed although God is its true agent, and assigns misguidance to those who embody it although He misleads by His decree; cited verses affirm His exclusive control of guidance and misguidance. | mentions 58:14, 18:17, 7:186
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r33] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الفرقة القدرية | rejects | Ibn Kathir rejects the Qadari claim that servants independently choose and cause guidance or misguidance: clear verses make God alone their controller, while innovators follow ambiguous passages and leave clear evidence. | mentions 18:17, 7:186
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r34] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet warns that people who follow ambiguous verses are those named by God as having deviation in their hearts; Ibn Kathir says the Qurʾan gives

no valid proof for innovation, since it has no contradiction and distinguishes guidance from error. | mentions 3:7
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r35] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r36] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · وائل بن حجر | reports | Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r37] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet said amin loudly enough for the first row to hear; Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah add that the mosque resounded, and al-Daraqutni calls the chain hasan.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r38] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بلال | reports | Bilal asked the Prophet not to say amin before him.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r39] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan and Jaʿfar al-Sadiq are reported to pronounce amin with a doubled mīm, like the Qurʾanic word in 5:2. | mentions 5:2
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r4] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الربيع بن أنس | reports | Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, through Abu Jaʿfar, identifies those favored as the prophets.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r40] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Saying amin is recommended outside prayer and especially within it, whether alone, imam, or follower; the sound reports promise forgiveness when one's amin coincides with the angels'.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r41] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | In the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet says that when the imam says amin, worshippers should say it; agreement with the angels' amin brings forgiveness of prior sins.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r42] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | The matching between a worshipper's amin and the angels' may mean matching in time, in the response received, or in sincerity.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r43] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو موسى | reports | A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r44] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.”
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r45] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and Hilal ibn Kaysan are reported to call amin one of God's names, but Ibn al-ʿArabi says the Prophetic report from Ibn ʿAbbas for this is unsound.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r46] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أصحاب مالك | reports | Malik's companions say the imam does not say amin but the follower does, citing Abu Hurayra's report that followers should say it when the imam reaches “nor the astray”; Ibn Kathir counters with reports that the Prophet himself said amin.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r47] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القول الجديد | reports | The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r48] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القول القديم | reports | The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r49] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r5] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas, through Ibn Jurayj, and Mujahid identify the favored people as believers.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r50] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عائشة | reports | A report from ʿAisha says Jews envy Muslims for Friday, the qibla, and saying amin behind the imam; Ibn Majah's wording adds greeting and amin.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r51] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | A report urges frequent amin because Jews envy Muslims for it; Ibn Kathir notes its chain contains the weak Talha ibn ʿAmr.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r52] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | Ibn Mardawayh transmits from Abu Hurayra a Prophetic report calling amin the Lord of the worlds' seal upon His believing servants.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r53] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أنس | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet was given amin in prayer and supplication; only Moses had it earlier, with Harun saying amin to Moses' prayer, so supplications should end with amin for acceptance.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r54] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it. | mentions 10:88, 10:89
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r55] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's request not to be preceded in amin.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r56] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | A report through Kaʿb says that when the imam says amin and the amins of earth and heaven coincide, God forgives the worshipper; one who omits amin is compared to a warrior whose lot was not drawn.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r6] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · وكيع | reports | Wakiʿ identifies those favored as Muslims.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r7] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam identifies them as the Prophet and those with him.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r8] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | prefers | Ibn Kathir prefers the earlier Ibn ʿAbbas account because it is broader and more comprehensive.
[IBNKATHIR:1:7/r9] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read ghayr in the genitive as an adjective modifying the path.
[BURHAN:v1p155/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The science of ambiguous identities has dedicated books by al-Suhayli and his student Ibn ʿAsakir, and was also studied among the early generations.
[BURHAN:v1p155/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The people blessed in the Fatiha are identified elsewhere as prophets, truthful people, martyrs, and righteous people.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa is the Mother of the Book because it contains all three fields: monotheism through 1:4, rulings in 1:5, and reminder from 1:6 onward.
[BURHAN:v1p182/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Sura endings, like openings, conclude with apt meanings and signal that the discourse has ended, releasing the listener's anticipation of what comes next.
[BURHAN:v1p182/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The Fatiha closing spells out the highest request: faith and its blessings, preserved from sins that bring God's anger and from deviation beyond His limits.
[BURHAN:v1p260#2/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · بعض الأئمة | reports | Some imams say al-Fatiha affirms lordship, seeks guidance in Islam, and asks protection from Judaism and Christianity.
[BURHAN:v1p352/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | One classification calls a stop sufficient when the next verse has verbal attachment, good and sufficient when attachment is semantic, complete when neither holds, and bad when the sense conflicts; 1:6 continues verbally into 1:7.
[BURHAN:v1p359/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The author says the familiar labels for stop quality are not a complete, sound classification and have produced confusion in books on pauses.
[BURHAN:v1p359/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A forced pause is caused only by running out of breath and is not restricted to particular places; examples include Ḥamza pausing within words or before a genitive complement. | mentions 2:207
[BURHAN:v1p359/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | An optional pause is preferable and is classified by how the two parts of the statement depend on each other.
[BURHAN:v1p359/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An incomplete pause leaves the preceding part sufficient but the following part dependent; one may stop at “straight,” but cannot begin with “the path of those.” | mentions 1:7
[BURHAN:v1p359/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | The author raises the possible objection that an omitted verb could be supplied to govern “the path,” leaving the answer beyond this excerpt.
[BURHAN:v1p73/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Qur'anic verse endings use either identical letters or letters close in sound; examples include the matched moon and two nearly matched Fatiha endings.
[BURHAN:v1p73/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Because sajʿ strictly requires matching letters, the close-but-not-identical endings in these examples do not count as sajʿ even for those who apply that term to Qur'an.
[BURHAN:v1p73/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala and makes the rest of 1:7 one verse; Abu Hanifa omits the basmala and divides its two phrases. Both count seven verses, but al-Shafiʿi's division better preserves the endings because anʿamta ʿalayhim does not match prior endings.
[BURHAN:v2p195/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | The blessed people are clarified by 4:69 as prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous; this broader verse is the best explanation of the Fatiha phrase. | mentions 4:69
[BURHAN:v2p195/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Wanting steadfastness on the straight path is itself obedience to God and His Messenger, since guidance to that path entails the obedience that places one with the blessed.
[BURHAN:v2p195/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A phrase may be assigned to a more fitting referent than its apparent one; examples include naming the Fatiha the seven oft-repeated verses though all Qur'an is described as repeated.
[BURHAN:v2p455/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A substitute can m

ake praise more forceful by stating a general description first and then naming its specific instance.
[BURHAN:v2p455/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Part and inclusion substitutes clarify and specify an antecedent by naming it twice, first generally and then particularly; the forelock example adds its quality as the reason for seizing it. | mentions 26:47
[BURHAN:v2p455/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A definite noun may be replaced by another definite noun, as in the Fatiha's repeated mention of the straight path.
[BURHAN:v3p239#4/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Putting those under wrath before those astray may convey disparagement: Jews preceded Christians historically and were nearer to the Muslims.
[BURHAN:v3p322/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The sūrah then shifts from direct address in “You bestowed favor” back to third-person wording, saying “not those who incurred anger” rather than “those with whom You were angry.” | mentions 1:7
[BURHAN:v3p325/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · التنوخي والخفاجي وابن الأثير | reports | Al-Tanūkhī, al-Khafājī, Ibn al-Athīr, and others classify the passive “those who incurred anger” after direct address as a shift of style.
[BURHAN:v3p325/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · السكاكي | reports | Al-Sakkākī’s account places all six kinds in the final category of iltifāt, the shift by implication.
[BURHAN:v3p326/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101
[BURHAN:v3p354/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The four broken plural forms of paucity and the two sound plurals are inherently paucity forms; other plurals may indicate few or many as context determines, as Qur'anic examples show.
[BURHAN:v4p292/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In الذين أنعمت عليهم غير المغضوب عليهم, غضب is the single opposite of blessing: the first group is believers and the second disbelievers.
[BURHAN:v4p355/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | لا can also be a coordinating particle, sharing the preceding word’s case while denying the second member what is affirmed of the first.
[BURHAN:v4p355/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | After a conjunction preceded by negation or prohibition, extra لا reinforces the negation; he classifies لا in this verse that way.
[BURHAN:v4p355/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda explains the added لا as preventing the mistaken reading that those astray are the same people as those under wrath.
[BURHAN:v4p355/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is that لا prevents readers from treating الضالين as coordinated directly with الذين.
[BURHAN:v4p58/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Good is attributed to God in the language of blessing and what is in His hand, while evil is omitted from such attribution as a matter of reverence; this is the sense of evil not being toward Him.
[NASHR:v1p227/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah.
[NASHR:v1p229/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | A pause on an incomplete fragment such as “bi-smi,” “al-ḥamdu,” or “rabbi” leaves the utterance unfinished and without an intelligible meaning.
[NASHR:v1p234/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | rejects | Sajawandi's mark lā means that one should not begin with the following words; it does not make stopping on the preceding phrase blameworthy, as some imitators assume.
[NASHR:v1p234/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · author | rejects | Stopping deliberately at ghayr or alladhīna is unanimously forbidden because the first is in construct and the second is connected; Sajawandi's lā forbids beginning there, not stopping before it.
[NASHR:v1p272/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · يعقوب | reports | Yaqub pronounces the hāʾ of dual and plural pronouns with ḍamma after silent yāʾ; Hamza agrees for ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim.
[NASHR:v1p272/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن كثير وأبو جعفر وقالون | reports | Before a following vowel, Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar join plural mīm with a wāw; Qalun varies by route, with many authorities selecting sukūn via Abu Nishit and others selecting ṣila via al-Hulwani.
[NASHR:v1p332/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن سوار | reports | Ibn Sawwar reports differing lengths for separated madd: some Hijazi and Basran routes articulate without lengthening, while Hamza, al-Aʿsha, and Qutayba use full length; the rest use a lesser extension. He calls madd before hamza or idghām especially good.
[NASHR:v1p332/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · علي بن فارس | reports | Ali b. Faris says Hijazi and Basran readers, al-Wali from Hafs, and Qutayba do not extend one letter for another; the remaining readers use full madd, longest with Hamza and al-Aʿsha.
[NASHR:v1p332/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو علي المالكي | reports | Abu Ali al-Maliki ranks Hamza, al-Aʿsha, and Ibn Amir as longest in separated madd, followed by Asim outside al-Aʿsha's route, then al-Kisa'i, though Qutayba is longest among al-Kisa'i's transmitters.
[NASHR:v1p332/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن مهران | reports | In al-Mabsut, Ibn Mihran says Abu Jaʿfar, Nafi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Yaqub do not extend across words; listed others do, with Warsh longest, followed by Hamza and Asim via al-Aʿsha. No one disputes extending within one word, though degrees differ.
[NASHR:v1p47/r10] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن كثير | reports | Khalil transmits from Ibn Kathir accusative ghayra al-maghḍūb, judged sound as a circumstantial phrase or adjective.
[NASHR:v1p47/r11] NASHR, d. 833 · أيوب السختياني | reports | Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani reads al-ḍāllīn with an open hamza in place of the alif, a rare feature in Arabic speech.
[NASHR:v1p47/r12] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Maki deems these noncanonical-imam readings permissible when reliably transmitted, since each has a sound Arabic analysis and agrees with the codex spelling; Ibn al-Jazari says others also share some forms.
[NASHR:v1p49/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو وحمزة | reports | Abu Amr, and also Hamza, read ṣirāṭ with a pure zāy; sibilants may substitute for one another, and the reading fits the rasm as does the sīn reading.
[NASHR:v1p49/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · عمر | reports | Umar reads ghayru al-maghḍūb in the nominative, supplying a predicate such as hum or ulāʾik.
[NASHR:v1p49/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · عبد الرحمن بن هرمز الأعرج ومسلم بن جندب وعيسى بن عمر الثقفي البصري وعبد الله بن يزيد القصير | reports | These readers pronounce the hāʾ of ʿalayhim with ḍamma and connect the mīm with a wāw.
[NASHR:v1p49/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · الحسن وعمرو بن فائد | reports | Al-Hasan and Amr b. Fa'id pronounce the hāʾ with kasra and connect the mīm with a yāʾ.
[NASHR:v1p49/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن هرمز | reports | Ibn Hurmuz also transmits two unconnected forms: ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm, or kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm; these and the standard three forms make seven dialect forms.

[ITQAN:v4p500/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Despite many later interpretations, the Prophet, Companions, Successors, and their followers identify those who incurred anger as Jews and those astray as Christians; Ibn Abi Hatim knew of no exegetical disagreement.
[ITQAN:v4p500/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Later commentaries often follow one author's specialty: grammarians multiply syntactic possibilities, storytellers collect reliable and unreliable narratives, and jurists expand into legal disputes unrelated to the verse.
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A further reading of guidance is to turn from everything besides God and wholly obey Him, even under Abraham's, Ishmael's, Jonah's, Moses', or John and Zechariah's severe commands. | mentions 6:153
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Calling the path that of people God favored, rather than people killed or punished, softens the demand and invites believers toward prophetic and saintly states.
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said that Surah Hud and its sisters made him gray because he was commanded to remain steadfast. | mentions 11:112
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Steadfastness means moderation between excess and neglect across natural and spiritual traits; the law sets this balance in action, speech, money, and character. | mentions 17:29, 25:67, 53:17
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet advised a would-be ascetic to fast and break fast, pray and sleep, because his self, wife, and visitors each had rights.
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | When Umar recited loudly to wake sleepers and repel Satan, the Prophet told him to lower his voice slightly; he told Abu Bakr, who prayed softly, to raise his slightly.
[BURSEVI:v1p11#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The author grades spiritual integrity by combinations of heart, action, and speech: complete inward and outward integrity is highest, while integrity in only one or two can harm its holder.
[BURSEVI:v1p13/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Those You favored is a complete substitution for the first straight path; favor here means the religion's beneficial gift.
[BURSEVI:v1p13/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو العباس بن عطاء | reports | Ibn Ata assigns knowledge to knowers, truthfulness, contentment, certainty and purity to saints, patience and compassion to the righteous, obedience's sweetness to seekers, and steadfastness to believers.
[BURSEVI:v1p13/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Another identification, matching 4:69, is prophets, truthful ones, martyrs, and the righteous. | mentions 4:69
[BURSEVI:v1p13/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | The path belongs to God by law and choice, and to servants as something they follow and obey; both attributions express its relationship to each side. | mentions 42:13
[BURSEVI:v1p13/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Attributing the path to God cuts off the servant's vanity; attributing it to the servant comforts and honors him, and removes Satan's hope of stripping believers of dignity. | mentions 63:8, 35:10
[BURSEVI:v1p13/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Repeating path indicates two journeys: the frightening way from servant to Lord, where caravans and mounts are lost, and the way from Lord to servant.
[BURSEVI:v1p14#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Not those angered or astray substitutes for those favored, describing the favored as free of anger and misguidance; ghayr can mean different from, not, or except. | mentions 17:73, 2:173, 51:36
[BURSEVI:v1p14#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Divine anger cannot mean its human beginning, so it denotes its end or effect, such as punishment, retribution, or painful seizure.
[BURSEVI:v1p14#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Misguidance means deliberately or accidentally leaving the sound path; sinners fail in action, while the ignorant fail in knowledge. | mentions 4:93, 10:32
[BURSEVI:v1p14#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both.
[BURSEVI:v1p14#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Anger fits the Jews especially because of their rebellious unbelief, aggression, killing prophets, and saying God is poor while they are rich.
[BURSEVI:v1p14#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mentioning both groups after the favored expresses full fear alongside the hope of favor; the Prophet says a believer's fear and hope balance.
[BURSEVI:v1p15/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Divine anger perfects the function of the left hand: mercy and severity have distinct effects, and severity completes what cannot be repaired by mercy. | mentions 39:67
[BURSEVI:v1p15/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Anger also purifies, like a doctor cutting a diseased limb or fire separating gold from lead and copper.
[BURSEVI:v1p15/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Bewilderment has blameworthy and praiseworthy forms; a beginner resolves confusion by identifying the goal, sound path, guide, helpful practices, and obstacles.
[BURSEVI:v1p15/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The bewilderment of advanced knowers is not a defect but appears after perfected knowledge, witnessing, and insight into the secret of existence.
[BURSEVI:v1p15/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النجمي | reports | The Najmiyya reading describes the two groups as people who missed divine light and wandered in the self's desires, nature's darkness, and imitation.

[ALUSI:1:7/r10] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الراغب | reports | Al-Rāghib defines bestowal as conveying beneficence to another rational being, so one does not say that someone bestowed a favor on his horse.
[ALUSI:1:7/r11] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A reported definition calls a blessing a benefit given by someone superior to a person without compensation.
[ALUSI:1:7/r12] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One view identifies those blessed as believers in general.
[ALUSI:1:7/r13] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view restricts those blessed to the prophets.
[ALUSI:1:7/r14] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view means the followers of Moses and Jesus before textual alteration and abrogation.
[ALUSI:1:7/r15] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view identifies those blessed as the Companions of Muḥammad.
[ALUSI:1:7/r16] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view names Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar as those blessed.
[ALUSI:1:7/r17] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | prefers | Al-Ālūsī prefers Ibn ʿAbbās’s report in al-Ṭabarī: the blessed include prophets, angels, martyrs, the truthful, and all who obey and worship God; other views restrict the class to some members. | mentions 4:69
[ALUSI:1:7/r18] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The unrestricted blessing embraces every blessing, in line with the verse saying that people cannot enumerate God’s blessings. | mentions 14:34
[ALUSI:1:7/r19] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One view says God blessed them by creating them for felicity.
[ALUSI:1:7/r2] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Apposition reinforces the predication, since it repeats the governing relation, and explains the straight path as the Muslims’ path, emphatically attesting to its rightness.
[ALUSI:1:7/r20] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view says God blessed them by rescuing them from destruction; a further view says the blessing was guidance.
[ALUSI:1:7/r21] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Using the active second-person verb is an appeal: since God has already bestowed favor, the worshipper asks Him to grant guidance too; the cited verse of poetry illustrates that God taught people to ask in order to give.
[ALUSI:1:7/r22] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The accompanying poem says that God would not have taught people to ask unless He intended to grant their hopes; al-Ālūsī gives no poet’s name.
[ALUSI:1:7/r23] ALUSI, d. 1270 · اللغويون | reports | The linguists list ten forms: hāʾ ḍamma/kasra with variable mīm and optional wāw or yāʾ. Attributions name Ḥamza, the majority, al-Ḥasan, ʿUmar b. Khālid/Fāʾid, Ibn Kathīr/Qālūn, al-Aʿraj, Muslim b. Jundub, Ibn Hurmuz, and al-Khaffāf from Abū ʿAmr.
[ALUSI:1:7/r24] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Ghayr is a matching apposition to alladhīna. Making it an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim is semantically awkward; the relative clause still contains its pronoun because the antecedent is not truly discarded.
[ALUSI:1:7/r25] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Treating ghayr as an adjective meaning different is weak: ghayr has become a noun and usually does not modify an expressed noun.
[ALUSI:1:7/r26] ALUSI, d. 1270 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh analyzes ghayr as an explanatory or restrictive adjective of alladhīna; al-Ālūsī explains that the relative is definite generically but can function like an indefinite when only an unspecified subset is intended.
[ALUSI:1:7/r27] ALUSI, d. 1270 · المحققون من علماء العربية | reports | Some authoritative Arab grammarians allow ghayr to become definite by annexation between two opposite definite terms, as in movement versus stillness; this analysis is adopted by those who rely on it.
[ALUSI:1:7/r28] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن السري | reports | Ibn al-Sarrī says ghayr becomes definite when annexed to a definite having only one opposite, since the contrast is then exclusive.
[ALUSI:1:7/r29] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The objection from 35:37 does not disprove this definiteness: ṣāliḥan may be a fronted circumstantial accusative, or ghayr alladhī may be an apposition to it. | mentions 35:37
[ALUSI:1:7/r3] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | An alternative analysis calls the second phrase an adjective of the first ṣirāṭ.
[ALUSI:1:7/r30] ALUSI, d. 1270 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; a noncanonical report attributes the same reading to Ibn Kathīr. It is best parsed as a circumstantial accusative governed by anʿamta, though other analyses are discussed.
[ALUSI:1:7/r31] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash permits the accusative as either a disconnected or connected exception if bestowal is understood generally.
[ALUSI:1:7/r32] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ rejects the exception analysis because ghayr then means siwā and the negative lā cannot be coordinated with it unless lā is treated as extra; al-Ālūsī notes the usage after wāw is unattested. | mentions 7:12
[ALUSI:1:7/r33] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الأخفش | reports | A report ascribed to al-Akhfash treats the exception as semantically negative, allowing lā to coordinate by meaning and removing al-Farrāʾ’s objection.
[ALUSI:1:7/r34] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الخليل | prefers | Al-Khalīl parses the accusative as governed by an omitted verb, aʿnī, and al-Ālūsī endorses him: exception is problematic and the circumstantial analysis requires an unpersuasive indefinite ghayr.
[ALUSI:1:7/r35] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some posit an ellipsis, supplying ghayra ṣirāṭ al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim, and offer several possible syntactic attachments; al-Ālūsī prefers the unelliptical straightforward syntax.
[ALUSI:1:7/r36] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The root of anger denotes intensity; the word is also used for a hard rock, a vicious snake, and a scowling she-camel.
[ALUSI:1:7/r37] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السعد | reports | In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge.
[ALUSI:1:7/r38] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السعد | reports | In his commentary on al-Kashshāf, al-Saʿd defines divine anger as the will to take revenge.
[ALUSI:1:7/r39] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | A definition in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid describes anger as a state of the soul followed by the spirit’s outward motion seeking revenge; another account calls it a change when the heart’s blood boils.
[ALUSI:1:7/r4] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One unusual transmitted interpretation treats the second path as different from the first, as if a conjunction were understood.
[ALUSI:1:7/r40] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | A hadith warns people to beware of anger, likening it to a glowing ember in the heart and pointing to swollen neck veins and reddened eyes; no grading or source is given here.
[ALUSI:1:7/r41] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s anger as His will to punish sinners, bringing punishment upon them as an angry king does to subjects under his authority.
[ALUSI:1:7/r42] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Following the early generations, al-Ālūsī affirms anger as an eternal divine attribute fitting God’s majesty without specifying how or claiming to know its reality, like mercy.
[ALUSI:1:7/r43] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The hadith God’s mercy preceded His anger means either that mercy’s effects are greater or that mercy appeared earlier.
[ALUSI:1:7/r44] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in the verses about being lost in the earth and God destroying deeds; in religion it means departing from truth. | mentions 32:10, 47:8
[ALUSI:1:7/r45] ALUSI, d. 1270 · أبو أيوب السختياني | reports | Abū Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads al-ḍāʾallīn with hamza, avoiding two adjacent quiescent letters although their meeting is permissible.
[ALUSI:1:7/r46] ALUSI, d. 1270 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd records the dialectal forms daʾaba and shaʾaba; this pronunciation is also found in ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd’s reading of 55:39. | mentions 55:39
[ALUSI:1:7/r47] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | The cited poem’s word fādaʾhamat exemplifies the same hamzated form; grammarians disagree whether the usage can be extended by analogy.
[ALUSI:1:7/r48] ALUSI, d. 1270 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | A reading with wa-ghayr in place of wa-lā is reported from ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr; the muṣḥaf’s mutawātir reading is wa-lā, which reinforces the negation implicit in ghayr.
[ALUSI:1:7/r49] ALUSI, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Aḥmad transmits and Ibn Ḥibbān grades as ḥasan a Prophetic report identifying the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians.
[ALUSI:1:7/r5] ALUSI, d. 1270 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad identifies the path with knowledge of God and understanding from Him.
[ALUSI:1:7/r50] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | Al-Ṭabarī transmits the same identification from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd; Ibn Abī Ḥātim says he knows no disagreement among Qurʾān commentators about it.
[ALUSI:1:7/r51] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Ālūsī also reads the general terms broadly: those erring in outward works, such as sinners, are under anger; those erring in belief are astray. The Prophetic Jewish and Christian identifications remain sound specifications of the general wording.
[ALUSI:1:7/r52] ALUSI, d. 1270 · من زعم | rejects | Some argue Jews and Christians are too mild a referent because atheists and polytheists are worse; al-Ālūsī rejects this reasoning in light of the sound Prophetic report and criticizes its disregard of hadith.
[ALUSI:1:7/r53] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الرازي | rejects | Al-Rāzī suggests that those under anger are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, analogizing to al-Baqara’s order of believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites; al-Ālūsī rejects the analogy against the Prophetic report. | mentions 2:1, 2:6, 2:8

[ALUSI:1:7/r59] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī says Christians are less culpable and closer to Islam, and a person who is merely astray may still find guidance.

[ALUSI:1:7/r61] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī argues that the Christian doctrine of Trinity is no worse than Jewish claims that God is poor, His hand is tied, and Ezra is His son. | mentions 3:181, 5:64, 9:30
[ALUSI:1:7/r62] ALUSI, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some explain the delayed mention of the astray by the rhyme of the verse endings; al-Ālūsī accepts this only alongside the other explanations.
[ALUSI:1:7/r63] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The blessing is directly attributed to God as a deferential appeal for guidance to those whose favor is established; anger is put in the passive and left unassigned out of courtesy in a humble request for kindness.
[ALUSI:1:7/r64] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن الأثير | reports | Ibn al-Athīr and al-Tanūkhī classify passivizing a verb after addressing its agent as an unusual kind of rhetorical turn; al-Ālūsī accepts it if turn means stylistic variation, and also defends the technical reading through al-Sakkākī’s definition.
[ALUSI:1:7/r65] ALUSI, d. 1270 · جبريل | reports | Abū Maysara reports that Gabriel taught the Opening to the Prophet and instructed him to say Āmīn after wa-lā al-ḍāllīn; the report is cited from Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Bayhaqī without a grading.
[ALUSI:1:7/r66] ALUSI, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī reports the Prophet’s instruction that the congregation say Āmīn when the imam recites the final words, so that God will love them; Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, and Ibn Abī Shayba transmit it.
[ALUSI:1:7/r67] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الحنفية | reports | The Ḥanafīs conceal Āmīn, following ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; the Shāfiʿīs say it aloud. The report of the majority’s loud recitation is interpreted as instruction or discussion.
[ALUSI:1:7/r68] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says the imam should not say Āmīn because he is the supplicant; this is also found in a less famous report from Abū Ḥanīfa, whereas the famous view is that he says it silently.
[ALUSI:1:7/r69] ALUSI, d. 1270 · عبد الله بن مغفل | reports | Reports from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mughaffal and Anas, cited from al-Kashshāf, say the Prophet concealed Āmīn.
[ALUSI:1:7/r7] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | rejects | A further interpretation makes the path adherence to obligations and Prophetic practices; al-Ālūsī dismisses it as a departure from the straight path.
[ALUSI:1:7/r70] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Āmīn is not part of the Qurʾān by consensus; a slight pause separates it from the sūra. Al-Ālūsī rejects Mujāhid’s contrary attribution as utterly false because it appears in no muṣḥaf.
[ALUSI:1:7/r71] ALUSI, d. 1270 · غير واحد | reports | Some authorities say that anyone who claims Āmīn is Qurʾān has committed unbelief.
[ALUSI:1:7/r72] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Āmīn is an Arabic particle functioning as a verb, built on fatḥa to avoid meeting two quiescent letters; its correct meaning is respond, while another view gives it a broader sense including a synonym.
[ALUSI:1:7/r73] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view says Āmīn is used for a broader meaning that includes respond and its synonym.
[ALUSI:1:7/r74] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A strange view derives the Arabicized word from the foreign hamīn because fāʿīl is not an Arabic pattern; a response says it may be a unique pattern with analogues, or originally short and lengthened.
[ALUSI:1:7/r75] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another unusual view treats Āmīn as a name of God because it contains a hidden pronoun referring to Him; al-Ālūsī finds this rationale even stranger.
[ALUSI:1:7/r76] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Readers disagree whether the alif in Āmīn is inherently long or short; groups support each origin.
[ALUSI:1:7/r77] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wāḥidī calls a doubled mīm a dialect form; another view calls it an error. Since Āmīn is a non-Qurʾānic supplication with a sound meaning, some say that pronunciation does not invalidate prayer.
[ALUSI:1:7/r78] ALUSI, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports a sound-chain hadith in which the Prophet tells Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that no Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qurʾān passage equals the Opening, calling it the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qurʾān granted to him. | mentions 8:24, 15:87
[ALUSI:1:7/r79] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī calls the sūra the Mother of the Book and a treasure of gnosis; he says some spiritual masters derive cosmic events, Muslim rulers’ names, their histories, and their fates from it, likening it to the Preserved Tablet of what appears in existence.
[ALUSI:1:7/r8] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim; this is also transmitted from ʿUmar and the Ahl al-Bayt.
[ALUSI:1:7/r80] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī closes by praying for the sūra’s lights to shine upon him and for access to its hidden secrets, declaring God the source of success and guide to verified truth.
[ALUSI:1:7/r9] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الشهاب | reports | Al-Shihāb takes the indefinite relative expression man as evidence that an indefinite name may be applied to God; al-Ālūsī calls this an evident confusion because the genitive is objective, not agentive.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p93/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The second ṣirāṭ is a complete appositive for the first; apposition reinforces the relation and explains the straight path as the path of Muslims, powerfully affirming its soundness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p93/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن عباس | prefers | Alusi prefers Ibn ʿAbbas's broad interpretation: prophets, angels, martyrs, the truthful, and everyone who obeys and worships God, as in 4:69; the unqualified blessing embraces God's innumerable favors. | mentions 4:69, 14:34
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p93/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Other explanations say God favored them by creating them for felicity, saving them from destruction, or guiding them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p93/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The first-person past tense “You favored” appeals tenderly to God's prior favor and asks Him to complete it by answering the prayer for guidance.

[ELMALILI:1:7/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | Elmalılı's final reading supplies no pronoun: unrestricted bestowal is a rhetorical indirect expression for bestowing the path.
[ELMALILI:1:7/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | This construal makes the path itself a supreme blessing, its bestowal a supreme divine aid, and the path theirs through divine gift and their following it.
[ELMALILI:1:7/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Receiving the route or means to a blessing secures repeated access to it, unlike receiving a single instance of the blessing.
