[ELMALILI:1:7/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The greatest path is the route by which divine aid arrives; without God's enabling, even a known and followed route may fail to reach its goal.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He asks God to make the community love those God loves, loathe those God loathes, and be joined to those who have attained.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He praises Muhammad as beloved by God and made beloved to creation, clothed with prophethood, raised from Maqām Ibrāhīm to Maqām Maḥmūd, leader of the pure, and seal of the prophets.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı asks for blessings and peace for the Prophet and for his family, companions, and followers.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله [ ص ] | reports | The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The straight path is that of people granted God's favor, not those who know truth and turn away in anger or those who never find guidance to truth.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله | reports | Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r5] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The guided path includes a desire to take the people favored by God as a good example.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r6] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The supplication seeks safety from explicit misguidance, represented by those under wrath.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r7] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | It also seeks protection from thought becoming confused by falsehood disguised as truth, which is the further form of misguidance.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r47] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The comprehensive reading makes the transition to the following request, for the path excluding those under anger or astray, apt to the context.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r1] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | He parses “the path of those You favored” as either an appositive or explanatory apposition for “the straight path.”
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r10] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الشيخ الجد | reports | The author’s grandfather applied the generosity appeal here to the Prophetic supplication, “as You blessed Abraham.”
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r11] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Asking to join the favored in rank also implies emulating the means by which they rose; it prepares disavowal of the other groups with hope and seeking refuge. | mentions 60:6
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r12] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Niʿma derives from naʿīm, comfort, ease of living, what suits a person, and luxury; its verb has the patterns of samiʿa, naṣara, and ḍaraba.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r13] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The noun can denote a good condition; its kasra form marks a state, and its scope expanded from sensory pleasures to beneficial non-sensory goods.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r14] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The requested favors are complete goods unspoiled by harm or a bad end, encompassing pure worldly benefits and, especially, benefits of the afterlife.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r15] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | These favors include worldly gifts and achievements, bodily and spiritual goods, and afterlife rewards; their central substance is guidance, including wise use of gifted goods.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r16] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The favored are recipients of complete favor, so their path fittingly explains the straight path: guidance itself is a blessing, and they were guided to it.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r17] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | One reading takes the favored as the best people of earlier communities, especially prophets and messengers; Islam answers the prayer by gathering and surpassing the sound guidance of prior laws.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r18] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | He also considers the favored to be prophets and messengers, whose state was fuller than that of their peoples; Jacob enjoined his sons to die as Muslims. | mentions 2:132
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r19] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Earlier communities were not all able to bear the fullest ideal; prophets nevertheless kept th

[IBNASHUR:1:7/r2] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The prayer first asks for a clear, easy way to salvation; identifying it as the way of the favored adds a further honor.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r20] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Whether the favored means prophets, their best followers, or earlier Muslims, the request is for a complete path suited to guidance available in each age.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r21] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Under each account of the favored, the request for guidance has the same possible force explained for the preceding verse: attainment, increase, or continuance. | mentions 1:6
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r22] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The prayer discounts benefits that are not ultimately pure: unbelievers enjoy real worldly gifts, but these bring anxiety about their end and punishment in the afterlife; the scholarly dispute over calling them favored is fruitless.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r23] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · القراء العشرة | reports | All ten readers pronounce ghayr in the genitive; syntactically it may modify the favored or stand in apposition, with the author preferring the adjectival reading.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r24] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | He prefers treating ghayr as an adjective: its descriptive sense outweighs apposition, which conventionally names the same entity as its antecedent.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r25] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Although ghayr is usually indefinite, it can describe this relative phrase because “those You favored” denotes no one specified group and is generic in sense.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r26] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · ابن هشام عن ابن السراج والسيرافي | reports | Ibn Hishām attributes to Ibn al-Sarrāj and al-Sīrāfī the account that ghayr becomes definite by negating a unique opposite; Ibn al-Ḥājib selects it for 4:95, and the author sees its result as close to the other account. | mentions 4:95
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r27] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh treats ghayr like an active participle meaning “different,” and similarly classifies mithl, siwā, and ḥasb; it becomes definite when permanence is intended.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r28] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The qualification seeks refuge from communities once guided who later corrupted understanding, disobeyed, privileged worldly desires, or failed to preserve their guidance.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r29] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The groups are broader than Jews and Christians: the first exemplifies deliberate religious rebellion, the second losing the way through misunderstanding; this reading makes the prayer meaningful after Islam superseded their religions.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r3] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The appositive restates the path generally and then specifies it, strengthening its meaning through a repetition comparable to emphasis.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r30] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | He says their earlier error was not yet deliberate and had not incurred divine anger; Jews exemplify the first group and Christians the second, but neither label is exclusive.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r31] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Adding the second negation advances from refuge against the graver fate to the lesser: escaping anger-inducing error does not cover lesser misguidance; the order also suits the verse endings.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r32] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Human anger is a psychic response to what displeases, producing aversion and harsh treatment; revenge may follow but is not essential, contrary to those who make it definitional.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r33] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Because literal anger entails change, which cannot apply to God, the attribution means its consequence—punishment, humiliation, or worldly exclusion—or a representational metaphor.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r34] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Early generations often left ambiguous attributes uninterpreted to focus on practice; later scholars used sound Arabic-based interpretation to answer false claims and clarify doctrine.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r35] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Divine anger is God’s treatment of those who oppose guidance, ranging up to the lasting punishment of polytheists and hypocrites; dislike is lesser, and both differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r36] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي | reports | A hadith says God dislikes gossip, excessive questioning, and idle talk; the author uses it to distinguish dislike from anger.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r37] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ethicists treat anger as the root of courage within the primary virtues; balanced force yields courage, while excess produces rashness and rancor and deficiency produces cowardice.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r38] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي | reports | When a man asked for advice, the Prophet repeatedly answered, “Do not become angry”; the author applies this to anger for oneself, which leads to injustice.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r39] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · بعض ملوك الفرس | reports | An unnamed Persian king said his reign endured because he punished according to the offense rather than according to anger.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r4] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | He finds no meaningful superiority between parsing the phrase as a matching appositive and as explanatory apposition; grammarians offer no decisive semantic distinction.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r40] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي | reports | The Prophet did not become angry for himself, but became angry for God when a divine sanctity was violated; the author approves anger used to protect public and religious interests.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r41] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Lā coordinates the straying with the objects of ghayr; contrary to the reported view of Makki ibn Abī Ṭālib, it is not needed to prevent attachment to the favored.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r42] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | He takes the extra lā as verbal reinforcement of negation after ghayr, following Arabic coordination under negation, as in 5:19. | mentions 5:19
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r43] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · السيد | reports | Al-Sayyid says lā prevents the mistaken inference that only the combined group is excluded, allowing one group to remain affirmed; the author distinguishes this from the semantic extra lā in 7:12. | mentions 7:12
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r44] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ḍalāl is missing the intended road through error, knowingly or unknowingly, like a lost camel; its use for religious or intellectual error is metaphorical.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r45] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · قالوا | reports | In religious usage, misguidance opposes full faith and ranges from neglecting recommended practice to unbelief; the author defines it as absence of guidance and notes sealing as its extreme form.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r46] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The angry group knowingly rejects religion or relies on wildly strained interpretations driven by desire; the straying group includes those who distort true religions through misunderstanding. Both are accountable for failing to seek truth.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r47] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | An ellipsis-like matching (iḥtibāk) implies both groups share both qualities, while assigning each its leading description shows that the strayers’ error is less severe.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r48] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي | reports | A report in al-Tirmidhī, which the author grades ḥasan, names Jews as an example of the angered and Christians as an example of the straying, not as exclusive referents.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r49] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Arab listeners knew Jews in Khaybar, al-Naḍīr, Medina, and Yemen, and Arab Christians such as Taghlib, Kalb, and parts of Quḍāʿa; both had altered their faith. | mentions 5:77
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r5] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الزمخشري | reports | The author reads al-Zamakhsharī’s account as finding emphasis in the apposition’s doubling and repetition of wording and syntactic government.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r50] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Islam’s straight path is clear in proof and sound in method, as the Qurʾān says; the law also distinguishes valid disagreement within Islam from disagreement that leaves it. | mentions 6:161, 6:153, 27:79
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r51] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says a qualified jurist who reaches the right answer earns two rewards, and one who errs earns one, acknowledging differing degrees of sound judgment.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r52] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | Most readers kasrate the hāʾ in plural and dual pronouns after a silent yāʾ to avoid heaviness; this matches the dialects of Qays, Tamīm, and Saʿd ibn Bakr.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r53] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · حمزة ويعقوب | reports | Ḥamza dammas the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim only, while Yaʿqūb dammas it in every pronoun of this class; the former follows a Quraysh and Ḥijāzī dialect.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r54] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · يعقوب | reports | Yaʿqūb reads every pronoun of this type with a preceding silent yāʾ and a dammated hāʾ.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r55] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الجمهور وابن كثير وأبو جعفر وقالون | reports | At pause-free connection before a vowel, most readers leave the plural mīm silent; Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Qālūn in one transmission lengthen its damma, a dialect also illustrated by Labīd.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r56] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · ورش | reports | Warsh lengthens a damma on the plural mīm when a hamza follows, but not before ghayr here; all readers leave the mīm silent at pause.
[IBNASHUR:1:7/r6] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Repeating a name before attaching its intended complement makes the named subject feel cherished; he illustrates this with Qurʾānic repetitions and al-Aḥwaṣ’s repeated verb. | mentions 25:72, 28:63

[IBNASHUR:1:7/r9] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The relative description of the favored and the attribution of favor to God honor them in contrast with the two rejected groups.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The mention of those angered and astray also alludes to the Qur'an's narratives about misguided peoples.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The sura's three aims together represent the Qur'an's original purposes, while its remaining material elaborates them.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | By contrast, Fatihat al-Kitab is a true annexation: al-Kitab here means the remainder of the Book apart from the sura called the Opening.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The names Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitab are established in the Sunna; “mother” denotes a thing's origin and source.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recited Umm al-Qur'an over a person suffering from a sting as a healing prayer.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A sound hadith calls a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an deficient.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | One explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it begins and opens the Qur'an, making it like its origin.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A second explanation is that the sura gathers the Qur'an's three main aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A third explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it contains the Qur'an's theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, including theology, prophecy, admonition, worship, transactions, morals, and law.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Those granted favor point to the good states of virtuous past nations and individuals; the angered and astray evoke the stories of deviant peoples.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Taken explicitly and by implication, the sura gives a general outline of the Qur'an's aims and prompts readers to seek their fuller detail as able.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Requiring al-Fatiha in every rak'ah preserves recollection of the Qur'an's purposes contained within it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha stands first as the Qur'an's preface, both for its core purposes and for the rhetorical excellence of its opening.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The majority agree that the sura is Meccan.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · كثير | reports | Many say al-Fatiha was the first sura revealed; Ibn Ashur rejects that chronology, placing the opening of al-Alaq and then al-Muddaththir before it. | mentions 96:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur's preferred sequence has al-Alaq, then al-Muddaththir, and then al-Fatiha revealed before it. | mentions 96:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Other accounts put Nun and al-Muzzammil before al-Fatiha; another says al-Fatiha was the first complete sura, unlike al-Qalam, which came in portions. | mentions 68:1, 73:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Some scholars say it was revealed when prayer became obligatory, and a report from Jabir ibn Zayd ranks it fifth in the order of revelation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet named it Fatihat al-Kitab and instructed that it be placed first in the Qur'an.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Its first placement does not conflict with earlier revelations: it was put at the front once enough Qur'an had accumulated to form a Book.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الحسن البصري | reports | Although the reciters and commentators agree on seven verses, Hasan al-Basri is reported to count eight; six is attributed to Amr ibn Ubayd and al-Husayn al-Ju'fi, and nine to an unspecified source.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Important guidance requires preparing listeners, stirring their attention, and removing stubbornness, false assumptions, and satanic impulses that block learning.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | As a Qur'anic preface, al-Fatiha models an Arabic literary opening that improves understanding and attentive reception.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Placed first by the Prophet's instruction, al-Fatiha trains readers in inner purification through its supplication from “You alone we worship” onward.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Following those granted favor expresses the desire to adopt a good example.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The prayer also expresses concern to avoid the plain error of those who incurred anger and those astray.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | “Those astray” additionally conveys concern that thought not become entangled in false claims disguised as truth.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | These aims help explain why al-Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur'an.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Because the Qur'an guides people and reforms both worldly and future life, listeners must prepare by removing stubbornness, error, and low impulses before receiving its wisdom.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The final distinction between the angered and astray wards off corruptions that can destroy sound knowledge or true revealed law.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p190#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The straight path metaphorically means the truth that leads its follower to God's approval, the goal Islam came to seek.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p190#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mustaqīm is the active participle of istaqāma and describes a route without bends; a straight highway brings travelers nearer without confusion or hesitation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p190#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains the straight path as the true religion and, in another report, the religion of Islam; Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the explanations together.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p190#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The definite phrase identifies the mentally understood unique straight path; truth is one while misguidance has many forms, and Satan's speech confirms this usage. | mentions 7:16, 10:32, 5:100
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p190#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | One explanation is that believers already received Islam and are taught this prayer to recognize God's favor, while later Quran and prophetic guidance continue to guide them.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p190#2/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | He prefers all sound beliefs and deeds, with guidance calibrated to each person's capacity; everyone needs it continuously to avoid neglect and deviation, and Islamic guidance continues through law and inference. | mentions 6:161
